title: Where to live next: senior housing choices in New Jersey
dek: From staying put to a continuing care community, here is what each option offers, what care costs in New Jersey, and what to ask before you sign.
keyFacts: Assisted living in NJ: about $104,520 a year (CareScout 2025 survey)
Nursing home semi-private room in NJ: about $153,300 a year
CCRCs register with the NJ Department of Community Affairs: 609-984-7905
Search affordable housing: NJ Housing Resource Center, 1-877-428-8844
Facility complaints: NJ Department of Health hotline, 1-800-792-9770
body:
Sooner or later, most of us ask the same question. Is this still the right place to live? For some people the answer is yes, with a few changes. For others it means a smaller home, a community built for older adults, or a place with care on site.

New Jersey has every kind of option, and the choices can blur together. This guide walks through each one in plain terms, with real New Jersey costs and the questions to ask before you sign anything.

Is staying home still the right call?

Staying put is what most people want, and it often works. The house is paid off or close to it. The neighbors know you. Your doctor is ten minutes away.

The question is whether the home can keep up with you. Stairs, a second-floor bathroom, a long driveway to shovel and a yard to mow all get harder over time. Many families start with small fixes: grab bars, a stair lift, better lighting, a first-floor bedroom. Our guide to aging in place in New Jersey covers those changes and the programs that help pay for them.

Help at home is the other half of the plan. A non-medical caregiver who helps with bathing, meals and errands costs a median of $86,944 a year in New Jersey for 44 hours a week, according to CareScout's 2025 Cost of Care Survey. That works out to roughly $38 an hour. A few hours a week is affordable for many families. Round-the-clock care at home usually costs more than assisted living.

A quick gut check

If you are staying home, ask yourself three things. Can I get in and out of the house safely in bad weather? Can I reach a bathroom on the main floor? Who would notice if I fell? If any answer worries you, it is time to plan, even if you never move.

What is a 55+ active adult community?

New Jersey is known for its age-restricted communities, and Ocean County is the best-known spot for them. Towns like Manchester, Berkeley and Toms River have large developments of single-level homes built for buyers 55 and older. You will find them in many other counties too, including Monroe Township in Middlesex County.

These are regular homes you buy and own. There is no care on site. What you get is a clubhouse, a pool, activities, and usually lawn care and snow removal handled by a homeowners association. You pay monthly association fees for those services, so ask what the fee covers and how often it has gone up.

Active adult living suits people who are healthy and independent and want less upkeep and more company. It does not solve a future care need. If your health changes, you would add home care or move again.

Condos and smaller homes

A condo or townhouse near your old neighborhood is the quiet favorite for many New Jersey downsizers. You keep your doctors, your church or synagogue and your friends. Look closely at the building's finances, the reserve fund and any special assessments planned for roofs, elevators or parking decks.

If you are selling a house to make any of these moves, read our guide to downsizing in New Jersey first. It covers the senior break on the realty transfer fee and what happens to your property tax relief when you move.

When does a continuing care retirement community make sense?

A continuing care retirement community (CCRC) offers several levels of living on one campus. You usually move in while independent, into an apartment or cottage. If you later need assisted living, memory care or nursing care, it is available on the same grounds.

The trade-off is cost. Most CCRCs charge a large entrance fee plus a monthly fee. Contracts vary a lot. Some cover future care at little added cost. Others charge market rates for care when you need it. Some refund part of the entrance fee to you or your estate. Others refund nothing after a few years.

New Jersey regulates CCRCs through the Department of Community Affairs (DCA). Its CCRC Program, in the Bureau of Homeowner Protection, carries out the Continuing Care Retirement Community Regulation and Financial Disclosure Act. Operators must register with DCA and give you a Disclosure Statement. That document covers the community's services, its fees, its finances and the terms of the contract.

Read the CCRC disclosure statement the way you would read a mortgage. Then have someone else read it too.

Ask for the disclosure statement early, before you put down a deposit. Have an elder law attorney or financial adviser review it with you. You can reach the DCA CCRC Program at 609-984-7905 with questions about a community's registration.

How do assisted living, memory care and nursing homes differ?

These three are often confused, and they serve different needs.

Assisted living is for people who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing or managing medications, but do not need round-the-clock nursing. Residents usually have a private apartment and share meals and activities. The New Jersey Department of Health licenses assisted living residences.

Memory care is specialized care for people with Alzheimer's disease or other dementias. It is often a secured unit inside an assisted living residence or nursing home. Staff are trained in dementia care, and doors are secured to prevent wandering. Ask exactly what training staff receive and how many aides are on each shift.

Nursing homes provide 24-hour nursing care. People go there for short-term rehab after a hospital stay, or long-term when their medical needs are high. The Department of Health licenses nursing homes too.

You can look up any licensed long-term care facility, along with its inspection information, through the Department of Health's facility search.

What does care cost in New Jersey?

New Jersey is one of the more expensive states for long-term care. These are statewide figures from CareScout's 2025 Cost of Care Survey, released in March 2026. Prices in your town may be higher or lower.

Type of careYearly costRoughly per month
Assisted living (private one-bedroom)$104,520$8,710
Nursing home, semi-private room$153,300$12,775
Nursing home, private room$173,375$14,448
Non-medical home care (44 hours a week)$86,944$7,245
Adult day health care (5 days a week)$26,000$2,167

Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care in any of these settings. It covers limited short-term skilled care after a qualifying hospital stay. When savings run low, New Jersey Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) program can help pay for care at home, in assisted living or in a nursing home. Our guide to MLTSS explains who qualifies. Not every assisted living residence accepts Medicaid, so ask before you move in.

How do I find affordable senior housing?

If your income is limited, there are apartments built for you, but most have waiting lists. Start early and apply to several at once.

  • The New Jersey Housing Resource Center. Run with the New Jersey Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency (NJHMFA), it is a free online registry of affordable and accessible housing across the state. You can search rentals and filter for units with accessibility features. Search at nj.gov/njhrc or call 1-877-428-8844.
  • Your local housing authority. Most New Jersey cities and many towns have a public housing authority. Many run senior buildings and manage Housing Choice Vouchers (Section 8). Call the authority in the town where you want to live and ask whether its senior waiting list is open.
  • Senior apartment buildings. Many nonprofit and faith-based groups run subsidized senior buildings. Rent is usually based on income. Each building keeps its own list, so you apply building by building.
  • Your county. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) can point you to local housing help. Call 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county's office on aging. You can also dial 2-1-1.

Keep a simple folder for applications. Write down the date you applied, who you spoke to and when to call back. Update every building if your phone number or address changes, or you can lose your spot.

What should I ask on a tour?

Tour at least three places. Go once on a scheduled visit and once unannounced, ideally around a mealtime. Bring a family member or friend and a notebook.

  1. Get the full price in writing. Ask for the base rate and every add-on. Many assisted living residences charge extra for medication help, incontinence care or a second person. Ask how much rates rose in each of the last three years.
  2. Ask about staffing. How many aides and nurses are on duty during the day and overnight? Is a nurse on site 24 hours? How long have the director and head nurse been there?
  3. Ask what happens when needs change. At what point would a resident be asked to move to a higher level of care? Who decides, and how much notice do you get?
  4. Check the license and inspections. Look the facility up in the Department of Health's facility search. Ask staff about any recent citations and what was fixed.
  5. Watch and listen. Do residents look engaged or parked in front of a television? Do staff call people by name? Taste the food. Visit the activity room at the time of a listed activity.
  6. Read the contract before you sign. Look for move-out notice periods, refund rules and fees for leaving. An elder law attorney can review it for a modest fee compared with what is at stake.

Once someone has moved in, help is available if problems come up. The Department of Health runs a 24-hour complaint hotline for health care facilities at 1-800-792-9770. The New Jersey Long-Term Care Ombudsman advocates for residents of nursing homes and other long-term care settings at 1-877-582-6995.

If you are having this conversation with a parent, our guide to the first conversation about care can help you start. The best moves are planned while there is still time to choose.

Not sure which level of care fits? Our senior living options guide starts from what your parent needs and links to detailed guides on assisted living, memory care, independent living and CCRCs.

faq.q: Who licenses assisted living in New Jersey?
faq.a: The New Jersey Department of Health licenses assisted living residences and nursing homes. You can look up a facility in its online facility search.

faq.q: Who oversees continuing care retirement communities?
faq.a: The New Jersey Department of Community Affairs runs a CCRC Program under the Continuing Care Retirement Community Regulation and Financial Disclosure Act. Operators must register and give prospective residents a disclosure statement. Call 609-984-7905 with questions.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for assisted living?
faq.a: No. Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care. New Jersey Medicaid's MLTSS program can help pay for assisted living for people who qualify, but not every residence accepts Medicaid.

faq.q: How do I find low-cost senior apartments?
faq.a: Search the New Jersey Housing Resource Center at nj.gov/njhrc or call 1-877-428-8844. Also call your local housing authority and your county office on aging (1-877-222-3737). Apply to several places, since most have waiting lists.

title: Selling the family home in New Jersey: a downsizing guide
dek: A realistic timeline, how to sort a lifetime of belongings, and the New Jersey tax rules every older seller should know before listing.
keyFacts: Sellers 62+ can claim a reduced NJ realty transfer fee on Form RTF-1
Since July 10, 2025, sellers pay NJ's graduated mansion tax on sales over $1 million
Federal home sale exclusion: up to $250,000 single, $500,000 joint
Senior Freeze is tied to your home; a move generally means starting over
Property tax relief questions: 1-888-238-1233
body:
Selling the house you raised a family in is one of the biggest moves of later life. It is a financial decision, a logistics project and an emotional goodbye, all at once.

It can be done well, at your own pace, with less stress than you fear. This guide covers the timeline, the sorting, the professionals who can help, and the New Jersey tax rules that catch sellers by surprise.

How much time should I give myself?

More than you think. If you have lived in a house for 30 or 40 years, plan on several months from the first closet to the closing table. Six months to a year is comfortable for most people. A sudden health change can shrink that, which is one reason to start early.

Here is a rough sequence that works for many New Jersey families.

  1. Decide where you are going. Pick the next home before you start clearing the current one. Measure its rooms and closets. That floor plan decides what comes with you. Our guide to housing choices in New Jersey can help you compare.
  2. Talk to your tax and legal people. Before you list, ask your accountant about capital gains and your attorney about the deed, the transfer fee and your estate plan. See our estate planning guide too.
  3. Sort the house. Work room by room, starting with the spaces you use least, such as the attic, basement or garage.
  4. Handle the leftovers. Decide what will be sold, donated, given to family or hauled away.
  5. Prepare and list. Make small repairs, clean, and talk with two or three local real estate agents before you choose one.
  6. Close and move. In New Jersey, most residential closings are handled with an attorney. Schedule the move for after you have the keys to your next place, if you can.

Where do I start with all this stuff?

Start small. One drawer counts as progress. A whole room on the first weekend is a recipe for exhaustion.

Use four labels: keep, family, sell or donate, and toss. Put sticky notes or colored tape on furniture. Give each box a label and a room before it is sealed.

  • Keep only what fits. If the new place has one closet where you had three, you cannot bring three closets of clothes.
  • Ask family early. Send children and grandchildren a list or photos of the furniture, china and keepsakes. Give them a firm date to claim items. Many adult children want far less than parents expect, so try not to take it personally.
  • Save the paperwork. Deeds, tax returns, insurance policies, wills, military discharge papers and medical records all go in one clearly marked box. Carry that box yourself instead of packing it on the truck.
  • Shred with care. Old bank statements and anything with a Social Security number should go through a shredder. Many counties and towns hold free shredding days. Identity thieves love a curbside pile. Our guide to scams in New Jersey covers more.
  • Digitize the photos. Albums are heavy and fragile. Scanning them lets every relative have a copy.
Every item you keep should earn its spot at the new kitchen table.

Should I hire a senior move manager?

A senior move manager is a professional who organizes the whole move. They help you sort, make a floor plan for the new home, arrange the sale or donation of what is left, hire and supervise movers, and often unpack and set up the new place so it feels like home on the first night.

They are especially helpful when children live far away, when a move is happening on short notice, or when sorting the house feels too heavy to do alone. Fees vary, usually by the hour or by the project, so get a written estimate.

The National Association of Senior and Specialty Move Managers has a find-a-move-manager directory where you can search by ZIP code. Before you hire anyone, ask:

  • Are you insured, and can I see the certificate?
  • Can you give me three recent clients to call?
  • Do you take a commission on items you sell for me, and from whom?
  • Who exactly will be in my home, and are they your employees?

Estate sale, donation or consignment?

Most homes end up using a mix of all three.

Estate sales make sense when there is a houseful of decent furniture, tools, collectibles or jewelry. An estate sale company prices everything, runs the sale over a few days and keeps a percentage. Ask what percentage, who pays for cleanup afterward, and how they handle security. Get the agreement in writing.

Consignment and auction can work better for a few valuable pieces, such as fine furniture, art or silver. Expect to wait for payment until items sell.

Donation is fastest. Charities such as thrift stores, Habitat for Humanity ReStores and local churches accept furniture and household goods, and some will pick up. Call ahead, because many no longer take older upholstered furniture or large televisions. Keep a list of what you gave, since you may be able to deduct it if you itemize.

A word of honesty from people who have done this: the brown dining room set that cost a fortune in 1985 often sells for very little today. Price the memories separately from the market.

What taxes come with selling a home in New Jersey?

Three rules matter most. Your closing attorney or title company calculates the fees, but you should know about them before you price the house.

The realty transfer fee, and the senior break

When you sell a home in New Jersey, the seller pays a realty transfer fee when the deed is recorded. The fee rises with the sale price.

Sellers 62 or older can claim a reduced rate. According to the state's Form RTF-1, the requirements are:

  • Each seller is 62 or older.
  • The home is a one- or two-family residence.
  • You owned and lived in the home at the time of sale.
  • You are a New Jersey resident.

Married couples and civil union partners who own the home as tenants by the entirety need only one spouse to qualify. Joint tenants must all qualify. The break is for individual sellers, so a trust, a business or an estate may not qualify. If the house is in a trust, ask your attorney before listing.

The reduced rates are much lower than the standard ones. On a sale of $350,000 or less, for example, the fee on the first $150,000 drops from $2.00 to 50 cents for every $500 of price. You claim it on Form RTF-1, which is notarized and recorded with the deed.

Do not leave money on the table

The senior rate is not automatic. Tell your attorney you are 62 or older and ask them to file Form RTF-1 with the deed.

The "mansion tax" now falls on sellers

For many years New Jersey's "mansion tax," a fee of 1% on homes selling for more than $1 million, was paid by the buyer. A law signed with the state budget on June 30, 2025, shifted it to the seller and made it graduated, starting with deeds recorded on or after July 10, 2025. The rates, as summarized by the law firm Bressler, Amery and Ross:

Sale priceRate
Over $1 million to $2 million1%
Over $2 million to $2.5 million2%
Over $2.5 million to $3 million2.5%
Over $3 million to $3.5 million3%
Over $3.5 million3.5%

The state's own transfer fee FAQ page had not been updated to reflect this change when we checked, so confirm the current rules with your closing attorney.

The federal home sale exclusion

Under IRS rules, you can exclude up to $250,000 of profit on your main home from federal income tax, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. You must have owned the home and lived in it as your main residence for at least two of the five years before the sale. On a joint return, only one spouse needs to meet the ownership test, but both must meet the living-in test for the full $500,000.

Long-time owners in North Jersey and shore towns sometimes have gains above those limits. Keep records of major improvements, such as a new roof, an addition or a kitchen renovation. They add to your cost basis and can shrink a taxable gain. A widow or widower who sells within two years of a spouse's death may still be able to use the higher limit, so ask your tax preparer about IRS Publication 523.

How does moving affect my property tax relief?

New Jersey's property tax relief programs follow the home, not the person. That matters if you are moving within the state. Our property tax relief guide covers the programs in full.

  • Senior Freeze reimburses increases in property taxes on a specific home. For the 2025 application, homeowners had to have owned and lived in their home since December 31, 2022, or earlier. A home bought after that date did not meet the rule. So a move generally means waiting until you have owned and lived in the new home long enough to qualify again. Ask the state how your base year would work at the new address.
  • Stay NJ is for homeowners 65 or older who own and occupy their home for the entire year as a principal residence. A move partway through the year can affect that year's benefit.
  • ANCHOR applies to the home you owned or rented and lived in on October 1 of the benefit year. Renters can qualify too, so a move to an apartment does not end your ANCHOR eligibility.

Before you sell, call the Senior Freeze information line at 1-800-882-6597 or the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233. Ask exactly how your move date affects each program. The answer can shape when you close.

What about the emotional side?

Expect grief, even if you want to move. The house holds birthdays, holidays and the people who are gone. It is normal to feel relief and sadness on the same afternoon.

A few things help. Take photos or a short video of each room before it is emptied. Let grandchildren pick one small keepsake. Plan a last dinner or a walk around the block with old neighbors. If you are moving away from friends, set up regular phone or video calls before you go. Our guide to staying connected has ideas.

For adult children, the hardest part is often patience. Your parent may need to hold each object before letting it go. That is part of the work. Build the extra time into the plan. Offer help, and let them make the calls on what stays.

If the job is too big for the family, our guide to senior move managers in New Jersey explains what they do, what they charge and how to check a mover's license.

Finally, give yourself credit. Choosing your next home while you are able to choose is one of the kindest things you can do for yourself and your family.

faq.q: Who qualifies for the senior realty transfer fee rate?
faq.a: Sellers 62 or older who own and live in a one- or two-family home and are New Jersey residents. For married couples owning as tenants by the entirety, only one spouse needs to qualify. Claim it on Form RTF-1 with the deed.

faq.q: Do I pay the mansion tax when I sell?
faq.a: For deeds recorded on or after July 10, 2025, the seller pays New Jersey's mansion tax on sales over $1 million, at graduated rates from 1% to 3.5%. Confirm the details with your closing attorney.

faq.q: Will I owe capital gains tax on my house?
faq.a: Federal rules let you exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 on a joint return) if you owned and lived in the home for two of the last five years. Gains above that may be taxed. Ask a tax preparer.

faq.q: Will I keep my Senior Freeze if I move to another NJ home?
faq.a: Senior Freeze is tied to a specific home. For the 2025 application you had to have owned and lived in the home since December 31, 2022, so a newly bought home generally does not qualify right away. Call 1-800-882-6597 to confirm your situation.

title: Driving later in life in New Jersey: safety, rules and options
dek: New Jersey's license rules, refresher courses that can trim points, the warning signs to watch for, and how to get around when it is time to drive less.
keyFacts: Most NJ drivers can renew online; a standard renewal costs $24
An approved defensive driving class can take 2 points off your MVC record
NJ Transit riders 62+ save 50% or more on one-way fares
Access Link paratransit: 973-491-4224, option 1
Disability placards (Form SP-41) must be recertified every 3 years
body:
For most of us, the car keys mean freedom. They get you to the doctor, the ShopRite, the grandkids' games and the Wednesday card game. In much of New Jersey, especially outside the cities, life without a car takes real planning.

Age alone does not make anyone a bad driver. Changes in vision, reaction time, medications and health can. This guide covers New Jersey's license rules, refresher courses, warning signs, how families can raise the subject kindly, and the ways to get around when driving no longer makes sense.

Does New Jersey test older drivers?

The Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) does not list any extra renewal steps for older drivers on its license renewal page. Most drivers can renew online, even if the renewal notice says to come in person. You can renew within three months of the expiration date on your license. A standard license costs $24, and a REAL ID costs $35.

Your new license arrives by mail, usually within two to four weeks. An online renewal takes effect right away, so print the receipt and carry it until the card comes.

A few things to know:

  • Do not let it lapse too long. If your license has been expired for more than three years, the MVC treats you as a first-time driver, with tests.
  • Update your address first. Change your address with the MVC before you renew online, so the new license goes to the right place.
  • Medical reviews can happen at any age. The MVC has forms for a physician or emergency room to report a medical emergency affecting driving (Form MR-4), and for police or a court to request a driver examination or medical evaluation (Form MR-5). These are triggered by health and safety concerns at any age.

Rules change, so check the MVC license renewal page before your renewal date.

Get your eyes checked on your own schedule

Cataracts, glaucoma and macular degeneration can creep up slowly. A yearly eye exam is one of the best things you can do for your driving. Tell the eye doctor how much you drive at night.

Can a refresher course help, and lower my insurance?

Yes, on both counts for many drivers. Cars, road rules and traffic patterns have changed a lot. A refresher course covers roundabouts and jughandles, blind-spot warnings, backup cameras and how medications and aging affect driving.

The AARP Smart Driver course is one of the best known. It is offered online and in classrooms. Course length and price vary by state. You do not need to be an AARP member, though members pay less. Prices vary by state, so check aarpdriversafety.org for New Jersey's current price.

Two possible benefits in New Jersey:

  • Point reduction. The MVC allows a two-point reduction on your driving record for completing an approved defensive driving class. It does not lower your MVC surcharge point total.
  • Insurance discount. Many auto insurers give a discount for completing a defensive driving course. Before you sign up, call your insurer. Ask whether the specific course qualifies, how big the discount is and how many years it lasts. Ask the course provider whether it is approved by the MVC for the point reduction too.
Think of a refresher course as maintenance for the driver, like rotating the tires.

What are the warning signs?

Everyone has a bad day on the road. A pattern is different. Watch for these, whether you are checking on yourself or a parent:

  • New dents, scrapes on the bumpers or mirrors, or scuffed tires from hitting curbs
  • Getting lost on familiar routes, like the drive to church or the pharmacy
  • Close calls, near misses or other drivers honking often
  • Drifting between lanes, or trouble staying centered
  • Missing stop signs, red lights or merging traffic
  • Confusing the gas and brake pedals
  • Slow reactions, or trouble turning the head to check traffic
  • Recent warnings or tickets from police
  • Feeling nervous, tired or overwhelmed after driving
  • New medications that cause drowsiness or dizziness

If the signs point to a medical problem, start with the doctor. Many issues can be treated: a cataract, a medication change or physical therapy for a stiff neck. Some hospitals and rehab centers offer driving evaluations by an occupational therapist. Ask the doctor for a referral.

How can I keep driving safely for longer?

Most drivers adjust long before they stop. Small changes cut risk without giving up the car.

  • Pick your hours. Drive in daylight and skip rush hour when you can. Glare and dusk are hard on aging eyes.
  • Plan the route. Choose roads you know. Use intersections with a traffic light and a green arrow for left turns, or make three right turns instead.
  • Check the weather first. Rain, fog and the first snow of the season are good days to reschedule errands.
  • Review your medicines. Ask your pharmacist which of your prescriptions and over-the-counter pills can cause drowsiness, and when to take them.
  • Fit the car to you. Set the seat so you can see over the wheel and reach the pedals easily. Adjust mirrors to shrink blind spots. A wide rear-view mirror or a seat cushion can help.
  • Stay limber. Gentle neck and shoulder stretches make it easier to turn and check traffic.

How can families raise the subject?

This is one of the hardest conversations adult children have with parents. Done badly, it can damage trust for years. Done well, it can make everyone safer.

  1. Ride along first. Take a few trips as a passenger, on different roads and at different times of day. Note specific things you see, not general worries.
  2. Pick a calm moment. Not right after a fender bender, and not at a holiday table full of relatives.
  3. Lead with respect. Say what you want for them: staying independent, getting to their friends, staying safe. Use "I" statements. "I was scared when the car drifted on Route 9" works better than "You can't drive anymore."
  4. Offer small steps first. Suggest an eye exam, a refresher course or a driving evaluation. Many drivers are willing to give up night driving, highways or bad-weather trips long before they give up the keys.
  5. Bring a plan for getting around. The fear underneath is isolation. Arrive with real options, phone numbers and a schedule of who can drive when.
  6. Bring in a doctor if you need to. Some parents will hear it more easily from a physician than from their children.

Our guide to the first conversation about care has more on talking through hard subjects.

How do I get around without driving?

New Jersey has more options than many people realize. Most work best when you set them up before you need them.

NJ Transit reduced fares

Riders 62 and older save 50% or more on a regular one-way fare on NJ Transit trains, buses and light rail, at any time of day. You can show any ID with your date of birth, such as a Medicare card, driver's license or passport. Note that NJ Transit Reduced Fare ID cards without a photo are no longer accepted as of January 1, 2026. Details are on the NJ Transit reduced fare page.

Access Link

Access Link is NJ Transit's paratransit service for people with disabilities who are unable to use local buses or light rail. It runs in the same areas and during the same hours as local bus service, and the fare is based on the local bus fare. You need an eligibility interview first. Call 973-491-4224 and choose option 1 to start. The TT line is 800-955-6765.

County senior transportation

Every county in New Jersey has transportation help for older residents, often free or low cost, for medical visits, shopping and senior centers. Rules and booking times vary, and many services need several days' notice. Call your county office on aging through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737, or dial 2-1-1, and ask what is available in your town. Some towns and senior centers also run their own shuttles.

Ride services and neighbors

Taxis and ride-hailing apps fill the gaps. Some services let you book a ride by phone without a smartphone. Local volunteer driver groups, churches and synagogues often drive members to appointments. Do the math, too. Once you add insurance, gas, repairs and registration, paying for rides can cost less than keeping a car you rarely use.

How do I get a disability parking placard?

If walking is the problem more than driving, a placard can help you park closer. The MVC issues wheelchair symbol placards and plates using Form SP-41. Qualifying conditions include, among others:

  • A severe, permanent disability that means you cannot walk without a cane, walker, wheelchair or another person
  • A severe, permanent walking limitation from arthritis or a neurological or orthopedic condition, or being unable to walk 200 feet without stopping to rest
  • Lung disease meeting specific test levels, or use of portable oxygen
  • A serious heart condition (American Heart Association Class III or IV)

A qualified medical practitioner must certify the condition on a prescription or official letterhead. Submit the application within 60 days of that certification. Mail it to the MVC Special Plate Unit, 225 East State Street, P.O. Box 015, Trenton, NJ 08666. Questions go to 609-633-8857. Placards must be recertified every three years.

A placard holder does not have to be the driver. A family member driving you to an appointment can use it while you are in the car. The MVC also has a separate Nursing Home Resident Parking Placard (Form SP-120) for facilities that transport residents.

Driving less does not mean doing less. With a little planning, the trips that matter most can keep happening. For outings that are easy to reach without a car, see our day trips guide and the free and discounted list.

faq.q: Does New Jersey require older drivers to retake the road test?
faq.a: The MVC's license renewal page lists no extra steps for older drivers, and most people can renew online. The MVC can require a medical evaluation or driver exam for anyone when a doctor, police officer or court raises a safety concern.

faq.q: Will a defensive driving course lower my insurance?
faq.a: Many insurers offer a discount for completing a defensive driving course. Call your insurer first to confirm the course qualifies, the size of the discount and how long it lasts. An approved course can also take two points off your MVC record.

faq.q: What ID do I need for NJ Transit senior fares?
faq.a: Riders 62 and older can show any ID with their date of birth, such as a Medicare card, driver's license or passport. Reduced Fare ID cards without a photo are no longer accepted as of January 1, 2026.

faq.q: How do I apply for a handicapped parking placard?
faq.a: Complete MVC Form SP-41 with certification from a qualified medical practitioner and send it to the MVC Special Plate Unit in Trenton within 60 days of the certification. Call 609-633-8857 with questions.

faq.q: How much does it cost to renew a New Jersey driver's license?
faq.a: A standard license costs $24 and a REAL ID costs $35, according to the MVC. Most drivers can renew a standard license online within three months of the expiration date.

title: What to do when a parent dies in New Jersey
dek: A gentle checklist for the first days, weeks and months, from death certificates and Social Security to probate and NJ inheritance tax.
keyFacts: Funeral homes usually report a death to Social Security for you.
A surviving spouse may get a one-time $255 payment; apply within two years.
Children, spouses and parents are Class A heirs and owe no NJ inheritance tax.
A will can't be probated with the County Surrogate until ten days have passed since the death.
body:
When a parent dies, the paperwork shows up at the worst possible time. Nobody expects you to handle it all at once. This checklist covers the first days, weeks and months in New Jersey, with the official offices to call. Take it one step at a time, and let a sibling or friend take some of it.

What does the checklist look like at a glance?

WhenWhat to do
First few daysFuneral home, death certificates, the will and key papers
First few weeksSocial Security, VA, pensions, banks and credit bureaus; start probate with the County Surrogate
First few monthsInheritance tax waivers, state benefits, final tax returns, and grief support

What should I do in the first few days?

  • Choose a funeral home. The funeral director usually reports the death to Social Security for you.
  • Order certified death certificates. Banks, insurers, pension plans and the Surrogate will each want one.
  • Find the will and important papers. Look for the original will, insurance policies, deeds, account statements and military discharge papers (a DD214).
  • Leave new deposits alone. Don't spend Social Security or pension money that arrives after the death until you know whether it has to go back.

Certified copies of a death certificate come from the local registrar in the town where the death happened, or from the New Jersey Department of Health, Office of Vital Statistics and Registry in Trenton. A certified copy has a raised seal. That is the version the Surrogate and most banks ask for.

The state's application (REG-27a) lets a spouse or partner, an adult child, grandchild or sibling, a parent, a legal representative, or anyone with a court order get one, with ID and proof of relationship. The state charges $25 for the first copy and $2 for each extra copy ordered at the same time. Mail it to Vital Statistics and Registry, P.O. Box 370, Trenton, NJ 08625-0370, or walk in at 140 East Front Street, Trenton, on weekdays. Local fees can differ.

How do I tell Social Security, and what can the family get?

Social Security says funeral homes usually report the death, so you may not need to. If there was no funeral home, or you aren't sure it was done, call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) with your parent's name, Social Security number, date of birth and date of death.

  • The month of death. Social Security's rules say a person must be alive for the entire month to be paid for that month, so no benefit is due for the month your parent died. Payments deposited after a death are normally pulled back from the bank, so keep the account open until that is settled.
  • The $255 death payment. A surviving spouse may get a one-time payment of $255. A spouse who lived elsewhere can qualify if they can get benefits on your parent's record. If there is no spouse, some children can get it, such as a child 17 or younger. Apply within two years, online through a my Social Security account or by phone.
  • Survivor benefits. A widow or widower can get monthly survivor benefits at 60, or at 50 to 59 with a disability, and age limits may not apply when caring for the deceased's child. They generally must have been married at least nine months. If your surviving parent qualifies for survivor benefits and another benefit, they choose the payment that works best for them. Social Security won't add the two together.

See also our guide to Social Security in 2027.

Who else needs to know in the first few weeks?

  • Medicare. Social Security handles death reports for Medicare too. If your parent also had a Medicare Advantage, Part D drug or Medigap plan, it's a good idea to call that company too.
  • Veterans Affairs. If your parent was a veteran or received VA benefits, call 1-800-827-1000. VA can also help with burial, a headstone and survivor benefits, and reporting quickly helps avoid overpayments.
  • Pensions. For a New Jersey state pension, call the Division of Pensions and Benefits at 609-292-7524 or use its online contact form. For a private pension or annuity, call the plan listed on their statements.
  • Banks, credit cards and credit bureaus. USA.gov advises reporting the death to banks, credit card companies, credit bureaus and other financial organizations. The three national credit bureaus are Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Also call any life insurance company that issued a policy.

You don't have to pay your parent's debts out of your own pocket. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says family members usually don't owe a deceased relative's debts from their own money. Those debts are paid from the estate, with exceptions such as a loan you cosigned.

Be wary of callers who say your parent owed money or ask for personal details. Our guide to scams in New Jersey explains the warning signs.

How does probate work at the County Surrogate's Court?

An estate is opened with the Surrogate in the county where your parent lived, as shown on the death certificate.

  • If there is a will. The executor named in the will brings the original will and a certified death certificate with a raised seal. A will can't be probated until ten days have passed since the death, though you can start the paperwork sooner. If the will has a self-proving affidavit, no witness has to appear. The Surrogate then issues Letters Testamentary and short certificates, which prove the executor's authority. Some banks want a short certificate dated within the last 60 days.
  • If there is no will. The closest relative applies for administration, with the surviving spouse first in line, then children. The Surrogate appoints an administrator and issues Letters of Administration. Administrators usually must get a surety bond.
  • Small estates with no will. If the estate is worth no more than $50,000, a surviving spouse or domestic partner may be able to use an Affidavit of Surviving Spouse instead of full administration. If there is no spouse and the estate is worth no more than $20,000, one next of kin may use an Affidavit of Next of Kin, with written consent from the other heirs.

Call your county Surrogate first, since fees and forms vary. If the estate is complicated or family members disagree, talk with an estate attorney. Our guide to estate planning in New Jersey explains wills, executors and powers of attorney.

Will the family owe New Jersey inheritance tax?

Usually not. New Jersey still has an inheritance tax, but Class A beneficiaries are exempt. Class A includes a spouse, civil union or domestic partner, children and grandchildren, and parents and grandparents. Siblings, nieces, nephews and in-laws are not Class A. When any tax is owed, it must be paid within eight months of the death, or interest is charged.

Because the tax is a lien on your parent's property, assets often need a waiver before they are released. When everything goes to Class A heirs, two short forms cover the common cases:

  • Form L-8 releases New Jersey bank accounts, stocks, bonds and brokerage accounts. The executor, administrator, or a Class A joint owner or payable on death beneficiary fills it out and gives it to the bank, not to the Division of Taxation.
  • Form L-9 is for real estate. Mail it to NJ Division of Taxation, Transfer Inheritance Tax, PO Box 249, Trenton, NJ 08695-0249, which then issues the real property waiver.

If anyone outside Class A inherits, or a trust is involved, these forms may not apply and a full return may be needed. New Jersey's estate tax no longer applies to deaths in 2018 or later.

What about final tax returns and New Jersey benefits?

Federal taxes. The surviving spouse or the estate's representative files your parent's final federal income tax return, due by the regular April deadline. On a paper return, write "deceased," your parent's name and the date of death across the top. A representative who is not a surviving spouse or court appointed needs IRS Form 1310 to claim a refund. The executor may also need to file New Jersey income tax returns; the Division of Taxation answers questions at 609-292-6400.

ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ. These run through one application. The 2025 instructions say that if the applicant died before October 1, 2025, they are not eligible. If they died on or after that date, a surviving spouse or personal representative can file, sign in that role and enclose a copy of the death certificate. Payments go to the spouse or the estate, never to the executor by name. See our property tax relief guide for the programs themselves.

PAAD and Senior Gold. The state's PAAD pages don't spell out a separate step for reporting a death. Call the hotline at 1-800-792-9745 to ask what they need, especially if your surviving parent is enrolled too.

Identity theft. If you think someone used your parent's information to file a tax return, the IRS identity theft form (Form 14039) has a section for a deceased taxpayer. A surviving spouse doesn't need to attach anything. A court appointed representative attaches the court certificate. If no representative has been appointed, attach a death certificate or a government notice of the death.

Where can I find grief support?

Give yourself time. If your parent was in hospice, call the hospice and ask about bereavement support for the family.

Your county office on aging can also point you to local grief groups, counseling and help for a surviving parent who now lives alone. Call 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county's office. If you were the main caregiver, our guides on caregiver respite and talking with family about care may help as you plan for the parent who is still here.

For the details, see our guides to getting a death certificate, choosing a funeral home, cremation and veterans burial benefits.

This guide is general information, not legal advice.

faq.q: How many death certificates should I order in New Jersey?
faq.a: Order more than you expect to need. Banks, insurers, pension plans and the County Surrogate each usually want a certified copy with a raised seal. The state charges $25 for the first copy and $2 for each extra copy ordered at the same time.

faq.q: Do I have to tell Social Security when my parent dies?
faq.a: Usually the funeral home reports it. If there was no funeral home or you aren't sure, call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213. No benefit is due for the month of death, and payments made after the death are normally taken back.

faq.q: Do children pay New Jersey inheritance tax?
faq.a: No. Children, grandchildren, spouses and civil union or domestic partners, parents and grandparents are Class A beneficiaries and are exempt. The estate may still need a waiver, such as Form L-8 for bank accounts or Form L-9 for real estate.

faq.q: Do I need probate if my parent had a small estate and no will?
faq.a: Maybe not. A surviving spouse can use an Affidavit of Surviving Spouse if the estate is worth no more than $50,000. With no spouse, one next of kin can use an Affidavit of Next of Kin for estates up to $20,000, with consent from the other heirs. Ask your County Surrogate.

title: Reverse mortgages in New Jersey: what seniors should know
dek: How a reverse mortgage (HECM) works for New Jersey homeowners 62 and older: the required counseling, the 2026 loan limit, real costs, the risks for spouses and heirs, scams to avoid and cheaper options to try first.
keyFacts: Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) are for homeowners 62 and older who live in the home as their main residence.
Every borrower must meet with a HUD-approved counselor first. Call HUD at 1-800-569-4287 to find one.
For 2026, the most home value a HECM can be based on is $1,249,125.
Costs include up-front mortgage insurance of 2% of the home value, 0.5% a year after that, and a lender fee capped at $6,000.
Borrowers must keep paying property taxes, homeowners insurance and upkeep, or they can lose the home to foreclosure.
body:
A reverse mortgage lets a homeowner 62 or older borrow against the value of the house without making monthly loan payments. The money can come as a line of credit, monthly payments, a lump sum or a mix. The loan is repaid later, usually when the last borrower sells, moves out or dies, and the home is typically sold to pay it off.

Almost all reverse mortgages in New Jersey are Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs), insured by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA). Before anyone can apply, they must meet with a HUD-approved counselor. For 2026, the most home value a HECM can be based on is $1,249,125. The loan can help some older adults stay at home, but it is expensive, and it comes with rules that can cost a family the house if they are missed. This guide explains how it works so you and your mom or dad can ask the right questions. It is general information, not financial or legal advice. A HUD-approved counselor and an elder law attorney can look at your family's own numbers.

Who can get a reverse mortgage in New Jersey?

You must be 62 or older, live in the home as your main residence, and own it outright or have a lot of equity. You also have to finish a counseling session with a HUD-approved HECM counselor before the lender can move ahead.

HUD's other rules for a HECM:

  • You cannot be behind on any federal debt, such as federal taxes or a federal student loan.
  • You need enough income or savings to keep paying property taxes, homeowners insurance and any condo or HOA fees.
  • The home must be a single-family house, a two to four unit home where you live in one unit, a condo that meets FHA rules, or a manufactured home that meets FHA rules.

The lender also does a financial assessment. It checks your income, assets, monthly expenses and credit, and whether you have paid property taxes and insurance on time. If the lender has doubts, it can set aside part of the loan to pay future taxes and insurance for you. That lowers the cash you get, but it protects the home.

  1. Call a HUD-approved counselor first. Call HUD at 1-800-569-4287 or use the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's housing counselor finder. Pick one yourself instead of using a name a lender hands you.
  2. Bring the paperwork. A recent property tax bill, your homeowners insurance declarations page, any current mortgage statement, and a list of monthly bills and income.
  3. Bring family. If your parent is married, both spouses should attend. Ask whether an adult child can sit in. Write down every question.
  4. Ask about the fee. Agencies may charge a reasonable fee, but the CFPB says they must tell you all charges before counseling and cannot charge you if you cannot afford it.

How much can you borrow with a reverse mortgage in 2026?

The amount depends on the age of the youngest borrower (or eligible spouse), current interest rates and the home's value, up to the FHA limit of $1,249,125 for 2026. Older borrowers and lower rates usually mean more money.

That limit is the most value a loan can be based on. It is not what you receive. You get a percentage of that value, called the principal limit, and closing costs and fees usually come out of it. HUD sets the limit each year. The 2026 figure applies to FHA case numbers assigned on or after January 1, 2026, up from $1,209,750 in 2025.

How you take the money matters too. On an adjustable-rate HECM you can choose a line of credit, monthly payments for as long as you live in the home, payments for a set number of years, or a combination. A fixed-rate HECM pays one lump sum at closing. A lump sum starts building interest on the full amount right away, so it is the most expensive way to borrow.

What does a reverse mortgage cost?

Expect several thousand dollars in up-front costs plus interest and fees that grow every month. Most borrowers pay these from the loan itself, which shrinks what is left for them and their heirs.

CostHECM rule
Up-front mortgage insurance2% of the home value, charged at closing
Yearly mortgage insurance0.5% of the loan balance each year
Lender's origination feeThe greater of $2,500 or 2% of the first $200,000 of value plus 1% above that, capped at $6,000
Servicing feeUp to $30 a month (fixed or yearly adjusting rate) or $35 a month (monthly adjusting rate)
Third-party closing costsAppraisal, title, recording, inspections, credit report and similar charges
InterestAdded to the balance every month, so you pay interest on interest

Say your mom's house in Morris County appraises at $500,000. The up-front mortgage insurance would be $10,000, and the origination fee would hit the $6,000 cap. Add title, appraisal and other closing costs and she could spend well over $16,000 before receiving a dollar. Then the balance keeps rising as interest, mortgage insurance and servicing fees are added.

A reverse mortgage is a loan you pay back with the house, and the bill grows every month.

The upside is the mortgage insurance. If the home sells for less than the loan balance, FHA insurance covers the gap. Your parent and the heirs do not owe more than the home is worth when it is sold.

What can go wrong with a reverse mortgage?

Most problems come from three things: unpaid property taxes or insurance, a move out of the home, and a spouse who is not on the loan. Each can make the loan come due.

Property taxes, insurance and repairs

Your parent still owns the home, and the title stays in their name. That means they still pay property taxes, homeowners insurance and flood insurance if needed, and they must keep the house in good repair. The CFPB warns that if these are not kept up, you could lose your home to foreclosure. If the lender orders repairs, you generally have 60 days to start them. In a high-tax state like New Jersey, this is the biggest risk. Run the numbers on taxes for the next ten years, not just this one.

Moving out

The loan generally comes due when the last borrower dies or moves out. A stay in a nursing home or other health facility of more than 12 consecutive months counts as moving out. So does living somewhere else for the majority of the year. If your dad might need memory care in a few years, a reverse mortgage may not last long enough to be worth the costs.

A spouse who is not on the loan

Sometimes only the older spouse signs, because the younger one is under 62. HUD rules can let an "Eligible Non-Borrowing Spouse" stay in the home after the borrower dies or moves to a care facility. The spouse must have been married to the borrower when the loan was made, must qualify under HUD's rules and must keep living there as their main home. Ask the counselor to walk through this for your parents by name.

What heirs face

When the last borrower dies, heirs get a due and payable notice. Under HECM rules, they have 30 days to buy, sell or turn the home over to the lender, and that can be extended up to six months to sell or get their own loan. To keep the house, they must pay the full balance. If the balance is more than the home is worth, they can sell it for at least 95% of the appraised value, and mortgage insurance covers the rest. Our guide on what to do when a parent dies covers the other early steps, and estate planning basics explains how to make wishes clear in advance.

Does a reverse mortgage affect Senior Freeze, Stay NJ or ANCHOR?

Your parent keeps the title, so they are still a homeowner. These programs look at ownership, residence, age and income, and they pay back part of the property taxes on the home. Ask the Property Tax Relief hotline how a reverse mortgage fits your parent's own application.

Homeowners 65 and older, or those receiving disability benefits, apply for all three on one form, the PAS-1. The deadline for the 2025 round was November 2, 2026. Stay NJ requires homeowners 65 and older to own and live in the home for the entire year as their main residence. The Senior Freeze has its own rules on age, how long you have owned and lived in the home, and income. Call 1-888-238-1233 with questions, or read our guides to Senior Freeze, Stay NJ and ANCHOR.

These programs work in your favor. They lower the tax bill a reverse mortgage borrower must keep paying. Before taking any loan, make sure your parent has applied for every one they qualify for. Our complete property tax relief guide explains how they stack.

How do you spot a reverse mortgage scam in New Jersey?

Be wary of anyone who calls a reverse mortgage free money, pushes you to buy something with it, or uses government-looking logos. A HECM is a loan from a private lender that you must repay.

Warning signs that the FTC and CFPB point to:

  • A contractor who suggests a reverse mortgage to pay for repairs, or who offers to arrange one.
  • Pressure to put the money into an annuity, investment or insurance product.
  • Ads that say "income for life" without saying payments can stop and you can lose the home if you move out or miss taxes or insurance.
  • Names, seals or logos made to look like a government agency. The CFPB notes the VA does not offer reverse mortgages, and some ads falsely suggest it does.
  • Fees, rates or total costs far above what other lenders quote.

Check that the lender and loan officer are licensed at NMLS Consumer Access, the national licensing database that New Jersey's Department of Banking and Insurance refers people to for mortgage lenders. Most reverse mortgages also come with a three-day right to cancel after closing. Send the cancellation in writing by certified mail.

To complain about a HECM, call HUD at 1-800-225-5342. For other reverse mortgages, report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov or 1-877-382-4357. Our scams guide covers the other cons aimed at New Jersey homeowners.

What are the alternatives to a reverse mortgage?

For many families, cheaper help exists. Start with tax relief and benefits, then compare a reverse mortgage with selling, a regular home equity loan or family help.

  • Tax relief and benefits first. ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ can return thousands a year. PAAD lowers prescription costs, and food and utility help can free up cash every month.
  • Sell and move. If the house is too big or too costly to keep up, selling may leave more money for your parent than a reverse mortgage would. See our downsizing guide and senior housing choices.
  • A home equity loan or line of credit. These have monthly payments, but the costs can be lower if your parent has steady income.
  • Family help. Some adult children pay the tax bill or a repair in exchange for a written agreement. Talk to a lawyer about how it affects the estate and Medicaid.
  • Smaller fixes. If the goal is to stay safely at home, our aging in place guide lists repair and modification help.
Questions to ask the counselor

How much would my parent get after all costs? What happens to my mother if my father goes to a nursing home? How much will we owe in five and ten years? Can we afford the property taxes for as long as we plan to stay? What would we have if we sold instead?

An elder law attorney can also review the papers before closing, especially if a spouse is not on the loan or Medicaid may be needed later. Our guide on finding an elder law attorney in New Jersey explains how.

faq.q: How old do you have to be to get a reverse mortgage in New Jersey?
faq.a: For a federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM), the most common kind, you must be 62 or older. You must also live in the home as your main residence, have substantial equity and meet with a HUD-approved counselor before applying.

faq.q: How do I help my mom decide if a reverse mortgage is a good idea?
faq.a: Go with her to the required counseling session with a HUD-approved counselor you choose yourselves (HUD: 1-800-569-4287). Bring her tax bill, insurance papers and monthly budget. Ask how much she would get after costs, what happens if she moves to a care facility, and whether selling or property tax relief would leave her better off.

faq.q: What is the reverse mortgage limit for 2026?
faq.a: HUD set the 2026 HECM maximum claim amount at $1,249,125 for FHA case numbers assigned on or after January 1, 2026. That is the most home value the loan can be based on. Borrowers receive only a portion of it, depending on age and interest rates.

faq.q: Can my parents lose their house with a reverse mortgage?
faq.a: Yes. The loan can come due and the home can go to foreclosure if property taxes, homeowners insurance or needed repairs are not kept up, or if the last borrower moves out, including more than 12 consecutive months in a nursing home or other health facility.

faq.q: What happens to the reverse mortgage when my dad dies?
faq.a: If there is no co-borrower or eligible non-borrowing spouse, the loan comes due. Heirs generally have 30 days after the due and payable notice to buy, sell or turn the home over to the lender, with possible extensions up to six months. They can keep the home by paying the full balance, or sell it for at least 95% of its appraised value if the loan is larger than the home's worth.

faq.q: Can I still get Senior Freeze or Stay NJ with a reverse mortgage?
faq.a: With a reverse mortgage the title stays in your name, so you remain the homeowner. You still must meet each program's age, residence and income rules. Ask the Property Tax Relief hotline at 1-888-238-1233 about your own application.

title: Affordable senior apartments in NJ: how to find and apply
dek: Section 202 buildings, public housing, Section 8 vouchers and state rental help: who qualifies, where to search, how waiting lists work and how to avoid waitlist scams.
keyFacts: HUD Section 202 apartments need one adult 62 or older and household income below 50 percent of the area median.
In Section 202, public housing and most voucher units, renters typically pay about 30 percent of adjusted income.
Apply for Section 202 at each building. Apply for public housing and vouchers through a housing authority.
There is no fee to get on a Section 8 waiting list. Housing authorities never ask for wire transfers or prepaid cards.
The NJ Housing Resource Center is a free statewide search for affordable rentals: 1-877-428-8844.
body:
Most affordable senior apartments in New Jersey come from a few public programs. HUD's Section 202 buildings are for households with someone 62 or older. Local housing authorities run public housing. Housing Choice Vouchers (Section 8) and New Jersey's State Rental Assistance Program pay part of the rent on a private apartment. In most of these, the renter pays about 30 percent of adjusted income.

The hard part is the wait. Lists are long, some open only for a few weeks, and some fill by lottery. The best plan is to get your mom or dad on several lists at once, keep the paperwork in one folder, and never pay anyone to apply. Every real program lets you apply for free.

What kinds of affordable senior housing are there in New Jersey?

There are five main types. Some are buildings you move into. Others are help that follows the renter to a private apartment.

ProgramWho it servesWhat the renter paysWhere to apply
HUD Section 202At least one adult 62 or older, household income below 50 percent of the area medianTypically 30 percent of adjusted incomeThe building's management office
Public housingLow income families, older adults and people with disabilitiesUsually 30 percent of adjusted monthly income, with a small minimum rentYour local housing authority
Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8)Generally extremely low or very low income householdsUsually 30 percent of adjusted monthly income, and up to 40 percent when you first leaseA local housing authority or the state list run by NJ DCA
State Rental Assistance Program (SRAP)Lower income New Jersey households, with a preference for heads of household 62 and olderPart of the rent, with state funds covering the restNJ DCA, when its waiting list opens
Income-restricted apartmentsHouseholds under the income limit for that buildingA rent set by the program for that unitThe property manager

Section 202 buildings are made for older adults who can live on their own. HUD pays for the buildings and helps cover rent, but it does not handle the leasing. You apply at each building.

Public housing is owned and run by housing authorities. It ranges from single homes to high-rise buildings for older adults. HUD's rule sets the tenant payment at the highest of 30 percent of monthly adjusted income, 10 percent of monthly income, or a minimum rent of $25 to $50 set by the housing authority.

Vouchers let your parent rent in the private market, with the subsidy paid straight to the landlord. The apartment has to pass inspection, and the housing authority's payment standard limits how much it will pay toward rent and utilities.

Income-restricted apartments include buildings financed with federal tax credits through the New Jersey Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency (NJHMFA) and units towns set aside under the state's affordable housing rules. Some are age-restricted. Rents are below market. Ask the manager for the exact rent and income limit before applying.

If your parent needs help with bathing, meals or medicine, an apartment alone may not be enough. Our guide to senior housing choices in New Jersey compares assisted living, continuing care communities and staying home.

Who qualifies, and what are the income limits?

It depends on the county and the number of people in the household. HUD sets new limits every year for each area, based on the local median income.

  • Section 202: household income below 50 percent of the area median.
  • Public housing: HUD's "lower income" limit is 80 percent of the area median, and its "very low income" limit is 50 percent. A housing authority can tell you the figure for your area.
  • Vouchers: HUD says households generally must be extremely low or very low income.

The dollar limits change every year, so look up the current figures for your parent's county on the HUD income limits page, or ask the building or housing authority before you apply. Each program also publishes its own limits when its list opens.

Income means everything the household receives. That includes Social Security, SSI, pensions, wages and other regular payments. Rent is figured from adjusted income, after deductions HUD's rules allow, such as for older or disabled household members.

Say your mom is a widow living alone on Social Security and a small pension. If her total is under the limit for her county, she may qualify for Section 202, public housing and a voucher all at once. That is a good reason to apply to all three.

Apply to more than one list. The first opening that comes up may not be the one you expected.

How do I find senior apartments near me?

  1. Search the NJ Housing Resource Center. This free statewide registry from NJHMFA lists affordable and accessible rentals. You can search for units with accessibility features. Help line: 1-877-428-8844. Go to nj.gov/njhrc.
  2. Use HUD's Resource Locator. At resources.hud.gov, choose "Find Affordable Elderly and Special Needs Housing" to see Section 202 and other HUD-assisted buildings on a map. Call each building you like and ask if its list is open.
  3. Find the housing authorities. HUD's public housing agency directory lists every authority in New Jersey. Many towns and counties have their own.
  4. Call the county. NJ 211 notes that each county's Area Agency on Aging handles housing programs for older adults. Reach yours through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737, or see our county pages.
  5. Dial 2-1-1. NJ 211 can point you to local housing help, any time of day. If 2-1-1 does not connect, call 1-877-652-1148.

Make a simple list as you go: building or agency, phone, whether the list is open, date you applied, and any confirmation number.

How do waiting lists work?

Every program keeps a list, and many are long. Some lists close for years, then open for a short window.

  • Lotteries. NJ DCA's statewide voucher list is closed. It last opened from January 17 to February 3, 2023, and 20,000 households were picked by random lottery. DCA's SRAP list last opened January 13 to 31, 2025, also by lottery. DCA posts new openings on its website.
  • Preferences. DCA gives the highest priority to veterans and their surviving spouses who have not remarried. Other preferences include homelessness, disability, domestic violence and local residency. SRAP also had a preference for heads of household 62 and older.
  • More than one list. HUD says that because of long waits you may need to apply to several housing authorities. Your parent does not have to live in a town to apply there, though a housing authority may require new voucher holders from outside its area to live there for the first 12 months.
  • Staying on the list. Housing authorities contact applicants in writing. If your parent moves or changes phone numbers, tell every list right away. A missed letter can mean losing a place.

Check the DCA voucher page now and then for the next opening. Note any dates on our key dates page too.

How do I apply, and what papers will Mom or Dad need?

Applications ask about everyone who will live in the home, their income and their rental history. HUD says a housing authority usually needs:

  • Names and dates of birth of everyone who would live in the unit
  • Current address and phone number
  • Names and addresses of current and past landlords
  • An estimate of income for the next 12 months, and where it comes from
  • Names and addresses of banks and any employers, so income can be checked

Expect to show proof later, such as a birth certificate, tax returns and benefit letters. Your parent will sign a form letting the agency check the information. Some housing authorities also visit applicants at home. If your parent is found ineligible, the agency has to say why, and your parent can ask for an informal hearing.

DCA's lists take pre-applications online only, and an email address is required. The form lets you create one if needed. If a disability makes the online form hard, DCA takes requests for a reasonable accommodation at 609-292-4080, option 9. The pre-application asks for Social Security numbers and income for everyone in the household.

It helps to gather papers before a list opens. Our important papers checklist covers what to keep in one place.

For the adult child helping out

Many older adults do not use email or feel nervous typing their Social Security number online, with good reason. Sit with your parent while you fill out forms on an official site, use an email you both can check, and save every confirmation page.

How do I spot a housing waitlist scam?

There is no fee to get on a Section 8 waiting list. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) warns that fake sites made to look like waitlist sign-ups often show up at the top of search results. They take a fee and personal information, and your parent never gets on a real list.

  • Housing authorities do not charge to apply.
  • They do not call or email to suggest joining a waiting list.
  • They never ask you to wire money or pay with a prepaid card.
  • Be wary of ads for "Section 8 apartments" that ask for first month's rent before you see the place.

Type official web addresses yourself, or start from a housing authority's phone number on HUD's directory. Report a scam to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Our guide to scams targeting New Jersey seniors covers other tricks to watch for.

What else can help while we wait?

A spot can take a long time. Other programs can ease the rent and bills in the meantime.

  • ANCHOR for renters. In the 2025 ANCHOR program, renters 65 and older with income of $150,000 or less get $700. Older adults have to file the PAS-1 application themselves, and the deadline for the 2025 round was November 2, 2026. See our ANCHOR guide.
  • Energy help. One application covers LIHEAP, the Universal Service Fund and weatherization. Our LIHEAP guide explains who qualifies.
  • Food and bills. Our food and utility help guide lists programs by type.
  • Veterans. Veterans and surviving spouses get top priority on DCA lists and may qualify for other help. See benefits for older veterans.

If your parent owns a home and is thinking about selling to rent, read our downsizing guide first. Selling can affect property tax relief, and money from a sale may count when a program checks income.

Her county office on aging, reachable at 1-877-222-3737, can point you to local programs. Apply to several lists at once.
