title: Snow shoveling help for seniors in NJ: programs and safety
dek: Which New Jersey towns and counties help older adults clear snow, how to sign up, what sidewalk rules say, why shoveling strains the heart and how to hire help safely.
keyFacts: A 2017 New Jersey law lets towns run free volunteer snow removal for residents 62 and older or with disabilities. Towns are not required to.
Camden County's senior and disabled snow program, as last posted, starts after 4 inches. Call 856-783-4808 ext. 5035 once the snow stops.
Sidewalk deadlines come from each town's ordinance. Lawrence Township, for example, gives owners and tenants 24 hours after the snow ends.
The American Heart Association says people with heart disease or its risk factors should have someone else shovel.
Counties declare Code Blue and open warming centers when forecasts call for 32 degrees or lower, or wind chills of zero or below, for two hours or more.
body:
If your mom or dad can't safely shovel anymore, start with a call to their town hall. Some New Jersey towns and at least one county run free or low cost snow removal for older adults and people with disabilities, usually with volunteers, students or county crews. Programs differ a lot, and many have sign-up rules, a minimum snowfall and limited spots, so call before the first storm.

If the town has no program, line up a neighbor, a local student or a paid service now. Heavy shoveling is hard on the heart, and the American Heart Association says people with heart disease or its risk factors should have someone else clear the snow.

Does my town have a snow removal program for seniors?

Maybe. New Jersey law lets towns create free volunteer snow removal programs for older adults and people with disabilities, but it does not require them. The only way to know is to ask your municipal clerk, senior services office or public works department.

A 2017 state law allows any municipality to set up a volunteer program that clears entranceways, driveways and the sidewalk in front of homes where someone 62 or older, or a person with a disability, lives alone or with young children. A town that creates one has to name a coordinator and publicize it, including on its website. Volunteers in these programs are protected from lawsuits over their work, except for intentional or willful and wanton misconduct.

Here are a few examples we checked on official town and county websites on November 1, 2026. Nutley's form and Guttenberg's notice are for the 2025 to 2026 winter. The Camden County, Hoboken and West Wildwood pages carry no date. Triggers, phone numbers and sign-up rules can change every year, so call before you count on any of them.

WhereHow it works
Camden CountyThe county's snow removal program for at-risk older adults and residents with disabilities starts after 4 inches of snow and only once the snow stops. Residents call the Division of Emergency Management at 856-783-4808 ext. 5035 (8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.) after each storm. Crews work in daylight, 8 a.m. to 3 p.m., in the order calls come in, with no set arrival times. Bring out your own salt if you want it spread.
HobokenFree help for residents 60 and older or with a qualifying disability whose main home is in a one or two unit building. The city turns the program on when snow passes 6 inches. Volunteers clear entranceways, sidewalks and driveways and can help with cars. Requests are filled first come, first served. Sign up with the city's online snow removal form. City Hall is 201-420-2000.
NutleyThe Shovel Out Seniors program (2025 to 2026 form) matches older adults and residents with disabilities with Nutley High School students. Students come after 3 inches or more and shovel within 24 hours after the snow stops. They clear the areas you ask for but do not clear cars or go inside. They don't shovel ice. You agree on a fee directly with the student. Questions go to the program coordinator at 973-284-4937 ext. 2116.
GuttenbergSnow plowing help for homeowners 62 and older who live in the home. For the 2025 to 2026 winter, the town asked people to register by calling 201-868-2315 ext. 152 and bringing ID, a property tax bill and a utility bill.
West WildwoodThe WW Shovels volunteer program helps residents 60 or older or with a disability who own and live in a one or two unit home. Applications are reviewed, so signing up doesn't guarantee a spot. It starts at 2 inches. Volunteers shovel and salt the main walkways within 24 hours after the snow stops, and the borough supplies the salt. Call borough administration at 609-522-4845 ext. 306.

If your parent's town isn't listed, ask the town, then the senior center. Our county pages list local offices on aging.

How do I sign my mom or dad up?

Call before the first storm and ask exactly how sign-up works. Some programs want you registered in the fall, and others only take calls after the snow ends.

  1. Call the town. Ask the municipal clerk or senior services office whether there is a snow program for older adults, who runs it and how to apply. If your parent lives in a county with a program, call the county too.
  2. Ask the key questions. How much snow turns it on? What gets cleared (the walk, the driveway, the sidewalk, the path to the car)? How fast? Is there a cost? Do I need to call after every storm?
  3. Have proof ready. Some towns ask for ID and proof that your parent owns and lives in the home, like a property tax bill or utility bill. Disability programs may ask for proof of disability.
  4. Put the number on the fridge. Write the program phone number on your parent's emergency info sheet so they, or whoever is checking on them, can find it fast.
  5. Have a backup. Volunteer programs fill up, and crews come in the order calls arrive. Line up a neighbor or paid service too, especially if your parent has a medical appointment or dialysis they can't miss.

If your parent lives alone, see our guide to checking on a parent who lives alone for ways to build a small circle of people who can help.

Do older adults have to shovel the sidewalk in New Jersey?

That depends on the town. Most New Jersey sidewalk snow rules come from local ordinances, and they set their own deadlines and fines. Check your parent's town code or call the clerk.

Ordinances usually give owners or occupants a set time to clear the sidewalk. Lawrence Township in Mercer County, for example, says owners, occupants and tenants must clear a path at least 24 inches wide within 24 hours after the snow ends or the ice forms. Other towns set different deadlines and fines, and an older homeowner is not automatically exempt.

Liability is a separate question. The New Jersey courts' model jury charge says a residential owner generally does not have to clear the natural buildup of snow and ice from the public sidewalk, but may be liable if their clearing makes things more dangerous. Commercial property owners can have a duty to clear it. These rules have exceptions, so for a specific situation, talk with a lawyer or the homeowner's insurance agent. This guide is general information and not legal advice.

Condos and rentals often work differently. Many associations and landlords handle snow removal, and the 2017 volunteer law excludes homes where a landlord or association is required to do it. Check the lease or the association's rules.

Is shoveling snow dangerous for older adults?

It can be. Heavy shoveling puts real strain on the heart, and falls on ice are a common winter injury. If your parent has heart disease, high blood pressure or past heart surgery, someone else should do it.

The American Heart Association warns that heavy shoveling may be as hard on the heart as a treadmill stress test. Risk is higher for people who don't exercise regularly and for people with diabetes, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, obesity, a history of smoking, or a past heart attack or stroke. An expert quoted by the AHA said people who have had bypass surgery or angioplasty should not shovel snow at all. The CDC also says people with heart disease or high blood pressure should follow their doctor's advice about shoveling.

If your parent insists on doing some of it, these tips come from the AHA and CDC:

  • Start slowly and pace yourself. Push or sweep the snow instead of lifting and throwing it.
  • A snow blower is easier on the heart. The AHA cites research finding heart rates around 120 with a snow blower and about 170 while shoveling.
  • Dress in layers with a hat, mittens and something over the mouth and nose. Wet clothes chill the body fast.
  • Stop right away for chest pain or pressure, lightheadedness or a racing or irregular heartbeat. Call 911 if it doesn't pass shortly after stopping.
  • Salt or sand steps, walkways and the driveway. The CDC says many cold weather injuries come from falls on icy sidewalks, steps, driveways and porches.

A railing on the front steps, a light over the walk and grippy boots by the door also help. Our guides to preventing falls at home and aging in place have more ideas.

How do I hire someone safely to clear the snow?

Hire early, get the deal in writing and pay after the work is done. A neighbor's teenager, a lawn care company or a plowing company can all work, as long as you know who is coming.

  • Book before the season. Ask whether they charge per storm or for the season, and what happens in a mild winter or a very snowy one.
  • Spell out the job. How many inches before they come, how soon after the storm, and exactly what gets cleared. Ask about salt, the front steps, the path to the mailbox and the space around the car.
  • Ask about insurance. A plow can damage a lawn, curb or garage door. Ask a company for a certificate of insurance. With a private helper, ask your parent's homeowner's insurance agent what is covered if someone gets hurt on the property.
  • Don't pay a stranger up front. Be wary of people who knock during a storm and want cash first. Pay by check or another traceable method after the job is done.
  • Keep them outside. Snow help rarely needs to come in the house. Several town programs bar volunteers from going inside at all.

Our guide on how to vet someone coming to your parent's home covers references, background checks and red flags in more detail.

What if the power goes out or it gets dangerously cold?

Have a plan for heat and light before the storm, and know your county's warming centers. Never run a generator, grill or camp stove inside the home or garage.

Code Blue. Under state law, counties declare a Code Blue alert when temperatures are forecast to reach 32 degrees or lower, or wind chills of zero or below for two hours or more. During a Code Blue, the county must open warming centers. Call 2-1-1 or check the county website to find them.

Generators and heaters. The CDC says generators belong outside, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent. Put a battery-operated carbon monoxide detector in the home. Keep space heaters at least 3 feet from curtains, bedding and furniture.

Register Ready. New Jersey's special needs registry lets residents with disabilities or access and functional needs, or their family and caregivers, share information with emergency responders so they can plan for them in a disaster. Sign up online through the New Jersey Office of Emergency Management or dial 2-1-1 for help. Registering does not guarantee help in an emergency, so a family plan still matters.

Keeping the heat on. Each winter, New Jersey's Winter Termination Program protects eligible households from electric, gas, water and sewer shutoffs from November 15 through March 15. Customers have to contact their utility to enroll and still owe the bills. Our LIHEAP guide explains help with heating costs.

The CDC also notes that older adults make less body heat and suggests people over 65 check the temperature in their home often during very cold weather. For ideas on keeping your parent busy and social through the dark months, see staying active through a New Jersey winter.

Who else can help with snow?

Call your county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 or dial 2-1-1 (or 1-877-652-1148). They can point you to local programs that change from year to year.

Senior centers and houses of worship often know who shovels for neighbors.

faq.q: How do I find free snow shoveling for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call her town hall and ask whether there is a snow removal program for older adults, then ask her county office on aging and local senior center. New Jersey lets towns run free volunteer programs, but not every town has one. Dial 2-1-1 for other local options.

faq.q: Are seniors exempt from shoveling the sidewalk in NJ?
faq.a: Not automatically. Sidewalk rules come from each town's ordinance, and many do not exempt older adults. Some towns that require clearing also run volunteer help for older residents, so ask the clerk about both.

faq.q: Who can help my dad if a snowstorm knocks out the power?
faq.a: Call the utility to report the outage, check that he has a working carbon monoxide detector, and keep any generator outside at least 20 feet from windows and doors. If he can't stay warm, the county will list warming centers during a Code Blue. Dial 2-1-1 or 911 in an emergency.

faq.q: Is it safe for a 75 year old to shovel snow?
faq.a: It depends on their health. The American Heart Association says people with heart disease or risk factors like high blood pressure or diabetes should have someone else do it. Anyone who shovels should go slowly, push instead of lift, and stop for chest pain or lightheadedness.

faq.q: What should I ask before hiring a snow plow service for my parent?
faq.a: Ask how many inches triggers a visit, how soon they come, exactly what gets cleared, whether they salt, how they charge and whether they carry insurance. Get it in writing and pay after the work is done.

title: Funeral costs and prepaid funerals in NJ: what to know
dek: What a funeral costs, your rights under the FTC Funeral Rule, how New Jersey prepaid funeral trusts and Medicaid rules work, and help from the VA and Social Security.
keyFacts: National median cost in 2023 (NFDA): $8,300 for a funeral with viewing and burial, $6,280 with viewing and cremation, not counting the cemetery.
The FTC Funeral Rule gives you itemized prices by phone and in writing, and lets you supply your own casket or urn at no extra fee.
New Jersey prepaid funeral money must go into a funeral trust or insurance policy within 30 days. Revocable trusts must be refunded within 14 days of a request.
Eligible veterans can be buried at no cost at Doyle Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Wrightstown, 609-738-2400.
Social Security pays a one-time $255 death payment to a surviving spouse or eligible child. Apply within 2 years.
body:
A traditional funeral with a viewing and burial had a national median cost of $8,300 in 2023, and a funeral with a viewing and cremation had a median of $6,280, according to the National Funeral Directors Association. Those figures leave out the cemetery plot, the grave marker, flowers and the obituary, so many families spend more. Skipping the viewing, as with a direct cremation or immediate burial, takes several charges off the bill.

In New Jersey you can pay for a funeral ahead of time, but the money has to go into a funeral trust or a funeral insurance policy within 30 days. The funeral home can't mix it into its business or personal accounts. Federal rules also let you buy only the items you want and get prices over the phone before you visit.

How much does a funeral cost in New Jersey?

There is no official New Jersey average. The best national figures come from the 2023 General Price List study by the National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA), a trade group. Prices vary from one funeral home to the next, so compare.

Funeral type (2023 U.S. median)Cost
Viewing and burial$8,300
Viewing and cremation$6,280

The NFDA notes those medians do not include a cemetery plot, opening and closing the grave, a monument or marker, or "cash advance" items the funeral home pays on your behalf, such as flowers, death certificates, clergy and the newspaper notice. Those can add a good deal to the final bill.

The biggest choices that move the price are burial or cremation, whether there is a viewing, how long it lasts, and the casket. Cremation is usually cheaper. In the NFDA study it was about $2,000 less at the median. Direct cremation and immediate burial skip the viewing and embalming, which keeps the bill down. A memorial service can still happen later at a house of worship or at home.

The Federal Trade Commission suggests limiting the viewing to one day or one hour before the service, and dressing your mom or dad in a favorite outfit instead of buying burial clothing.

Ask for the price list before you sit down with the funeral director. It is your right.

What rights do I have under the FTC Funeral Rule?

The Federal Trade Commission's Funeral Rule lets you buy only the goods and services you want and see itemized prices before you choose. It applies when you plan ahead and when you make arrangements after a death.

  • Prices by phone. A funeral home must give you price information over the phone if you ask. You do not have to give your name, address or phone number first.
  • A General Price List to keep. When you visit, you must get a written, itemized General Price List with every item and service and its cost.
  • Casket and vault prices first. You have the right to see a casket price list before you see the caskets, and an outer burial container price list. Ask about lower priced models that may not be on display.
  • No forced packages. You can buy items one by one. The only charge you cannot decline is the funeral home's basic services fee.
  • Your own casket or urn. You can buy a casket or urn somewhere else, including online. The funeral home cannot refuse it or charge a fee to handle it.
  • Embalming is usually optional. The FTC says no state requires routine embalming for every death. Refrigeration is often an alternative. Direct cremation and immediate burial need no embalming at all.
  • Cardboard or plain wood for cremation. No law requires a casket for cremation. A funeral home that offers cremation must offer an alternative container.
  • A written statement before you pay. You must get an itemized statement of everything you chose, with each price and the total. If the home says a cemetery or crematory requires something, the statement must explain that requirement.

Outer burial containers (vaults or grave liners) are not required by any state law, but many cemeteries require one. The Funeral Rule does not cover cemeteries without an on-site funeral home, or separate casket and monument sellers, so ask those businesses for written prices too.

How do prepaid funerals work in New Jersey?

New Jersey lets you sign a prepaid funeral agreement with a funeral home, funded by either a funeral trust or a funeral insurance policy. The funeral home must deposit your money in the trust or with the insurer within 30 days and may never mix it with its business or personal accounts.

State rules from the Board of Mortuary Science, part of the Division of Consumer Affairs, require every agreement to be in writing and to include:

  • The funeral director's name and license number and the registered funeral home's address and phone
  • How it is funded, and the name of the bank, pooled trust or insurance company holding the money
  • Whether the price is guaranteed (the funeral home must provide those listed items at no extra cost later) or non-guaranteed (your family may owe more at the time of death, or change the plan, if the money falls short)
  • A separate itemized Statement of Funeral Goods and Services Selected

Unless a plan is set up as irrevocable (see the Medicaid section below), it is revocable. The buyer can cancel, and the funeral home must refund a funeral trust within 14 days of the request. You can also move the plan to a different funeral home, which must happen within 10 days. That matters if your mom moves to be near you in another county. If a revocable trust has money left after the funeral, the surplus goes back to the buyer or the estate.

  1. Compare at least two funeral homes. Get each General Price List and compare the same items.
  2. Ask how the money is held. Get the name of the trust or insurer in writing, and look for proof the trust was set up. The funeral home must send it unless the pooled trust sends it to you directly.
  3. Ask if the price is guaranteed. Find out which items are covered and which are not, such as cemetery charges and cash advance items.
  4. Tell the family. Keep the contract with your parent's important papers and make sure the person who will handle the funeral knows it exists.

Check whether the contract covers any cemetery costs. The grave, the opening and closing, and the marker are usually bought from the cemetery. Cemeteries that are not run by a religious group are regulated separately, by the New Jersey Cemetery Board.

Does a prepaid funeral count against Medicaid in New Jersey?

Money in an irrevocable prepaid funeral plan generally is not counted toward Medicaid's asset limit. State rules allow an irrevocable plan only for an older, blind or disabled person who is applying for or getting SSI, Medicaid or General Assistance, or who reasonably expects to apply within six months.

Irrevocable means no refund while your parent is alive. You can still transfer it to another funeral home. Funeral homes may not use these plans to charge more than fair market value, and they may not set one up for someone who won't qualify for those programs.

New Jersey's Medicaid rules also exclude burial spaces, such as a grave, crypt or niche, for your parent and close family. Separately, a person may set aside up to $1,500 in burial funds (and $1,500 for a spouse) when that money would otherwise make them ineligible. That $1,500 limit is reduced by any irrevocable funeral funds and by the face value of certain small life insurance policies.

Medicaid rules are detailed, and a planning mistake can delay coverage. This is general information, not legal or financial advice. Before your parent applies, talk with the county board of social services or an elder law attorney, and read our guide to NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS.

What help is there for veterans' funerals in New Jersey?

An eligible veteran can be buried at no cost at the Brigadier General William C. Doyle Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Wrightstown, Burlington County, and the VA may pay a burial and plot allowance.

The state runs Doyle Cemetery for veterans whose last service ended under conditions other than dishonorable, along with their spouses and certain dependent children. The cemetery says there is no charge for the grave, its upkeep, a government headstone or niche cover, or a grave liner. The family still pays the funeral home to prepare and transport the remains. Military honors are provided for veterans.

  • Graves can't be reserved, but you can pre-register to confirm eligibility. Do it at the cemetery or any Veterans Service Office, or by mail.
  • At the time of need, the funeral director calls the cemetery. Have the DD Form 214 (discharge papers) ready.
  • Contact: 350 Provinceline Road, Wrightstown, NJ 08562. Call 609-738-2400. Office hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.

The VA burial allowance depends on how and when the veteran died. For a death that is not service connected on or after October 1, 2026, the VA pays up to $1,032 toward burial and $1,032 toward a plot ($1,002 each for deaths from October 1, 2025, through September 30, 2026), if the veteran was getting VA pension or compensation, died in VA care, or meets another listed condition. For a service-connected death on or after September 11, 2001, the maximum is $2,000. Apply on VA.gov or with VA Form 21P-530EZ. For a death that is not service connected, the burial allowance claim generally must be filed within 2 years of the burial. More detail is in our guide to benefits for older veterans.

Does Social Security help pay for a funeral?

Only a little. Social Security pays a one-time $255 lump-sum death payment to a surviving spouse, or if there is no spouse, to certain children. You must apply within 2 years of the death.

A spouse who lived apart may still qualify if they can get benefits on the record of the person who died. Children may qualify if they are 17 or younger, 18 or 19 and in school full time through grade 12, or any age with a disability that began at 21 or younger. Adult children who are not disabled do not get the payment. Apply online with a my Social Security account or call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). Our guide on what to do when a parent dies lists the other calls to make in the first weeks.

Who decides about the funeral, and how do I file a complaint?

Under New Jersey law, a person can name someone to control their funeral in a will or on a notarized state form signed in front of two witnesses. Without that, the right goes first to a spouse, civil union partner or domestic partner, then to a majority of the adult children, then parents, then siblings.

If your mom or dad has clear wishes, naming someone can head off arguments between siblings. It is a good thing to settle while doing estate planning. The person named cannot be someone who works for the funeral home, cemetery or crematory, unless they are a relative. If the person first in line doesn't act within 72 hours of the death, or can't be reached, the right passes to the next person in line.

If something goes wrong:

  • Funeral homes and prepaid plans. File a complaint with the State Board of Mortuary Science through the Division of Consumer Affairs, 1-800-242-5846 (toll free in NJ) or 973-504-6200.
  • Cemeteries. Complaints about cemeteries not run by a religious group go to the New Jersey Cemetery Board, also part of Consumer Affairs.
  • Price list problems. Report Funeral Rule violations to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Be wary of anyone who calls or knocks to sell a burial plan, cemetery lot or "final expense" policy with pressure to sign today. Our guide to scams aimed at older adults in New Jersey explains how to check a caller. For the next steps, see our guides to choosing a funeral home, cremation in New Jersey, getting death certificates and veterans burial benefits. In Essex County, see funeral homes and cemeteries in Essex. After the arrangements, our list of grief support in NJ may help.

faq.q: How do I find out what a funeral will cost for my mom?
faq.a: Call two or three funeral homes and ask for their prices over the phone, or ask them to send the General Price List. Under the FTC Funeral Rule they must give prices by phone, and you don't have to give your name first. Compare the same items, and remember the cemetery charges separately for the grave, vault and opening and closing.

faq.q: Can I cancel a prepaid funeral in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes, unless it was set up as irrevocable. For a revocable plan, the funeral home must refund a funeral trust within 14 days of the request. Irrevocable plans, used by people applying for or receiving Medicaid, SSI or General Assistance, cannot be refunded during the person's lifetime, though they can be moved to another funeral home.

faq.q: Should my dad buy an irrevocable funeral trust before applying for Medicaid?
faq.a: It can help, because irrevocable funeral money generally isn't counted as an asset. New Jersey allows it only for an older, blind or disabled person who is applying for or receiving SSI, Medicaid or General Assistance, or expects to apply within six months. This isn't legal advice, so check with the county board of social services or an elder law attorney first.

faq.q: Is embalming required in New Jersey?
faq.a: The FTC says no state requires routine embalming for every death, and refrigeration is often an alternative. Many funeral homes require embalming for a public viewing, so ask about a private family viewing or direct cremation if you want to skip it.

faq.q: Is burial at Doyle Veterans Cemetery free?
faq.a: Yes, for eligible veterans and their eligible spouses and dependents. The cemetery does not charge for the grave, its care, a government headstone or niche cover, or a grave liner. The family pays the funeral home for preparation and transportation. Call 609-738-2400.

faq.q: How do I claim the $255 Social Security death payment for my father?
faq.a: A surviving spouse or an eligible child (generally under 18, or 18 to 19 in high school, or disabled at 21 or younger) can apply online with a my Social Security account or by calling 1-800-772-1213 within 2 years of the death. Adult children who are not disabled cannot get it.

title: Cremation in New Jersey: costs, rules and what to expect
dek: How cremation works in NJ, who can sign for it, the 24 hour waiting period, what drives the price, and what you get back afterward.
keyFacts: New Jersey law bars cremation until at least 24 hours after the time of death on the death certificate.
Without a named agent, the right to decide goes to a spouse or partner, then a majority of the adult children.
No law requires a casket for cremation. Funeral homes that offer cremation must offer a simple alternative container.
NFDA's 2023 national median for a funeral with viewing and cremation was $6,280, not counting cemetery costs.
NJ crematories must track remains by two separate means, one of them a metal ID disc or similar heat-proof tag.
body:
Cremation in New Jersey starts with a funeral home. The funeral director collects the paperwork, gets the signed authorization from the person with the legal right to decide, and brings your mom or dad to a licensed crematory. By state law, the cremation cannot happen until at least 24 hours have passed from the time of death recorded on the death certificate.

The person who signs is usually the surviving spouse or partner. If there isn't one, a majority of the adult children decide together, unless your parent named someone in a will or on a state form. How quickly it happens depends on the paperwork and on whether a medical examiner is involved. The price depends mostly on whether you hold a viewing and service first.

TopicNew Jersey rule
Waiting period24 hours after death
Who signsNamed agent, then spouse, then adult children
Where it happensCrematory approved by the Cemetery Board
CasketNot required; a simple container is fine
EmbalmingNot needed for direct cremation

How does cremation work in New Jersey, step by step?

You choose a funeral home, sign an authorization, and the funeral director handles the rest. Here is the usual order of events.

  1. Call a funeral home. If your parent died in a hospital or nursing home, staff will ask which funeral home to call. Our guide to choosing a funeral home explains how to compare them.
  2. Make the arrangements. You meet or talk by phone with the funeral director, pick the services you want, and get an itemized written statement of what you chose before you pay.
  3. Sign the cremation authorization. The person with the right to decide signs it. The form also records the planned disposition of the ashes, if you know it.
  4. The paperwork is completed. The death certificate is filed and the funeral director gets a permit for final disposition. Cremating a body without that permit is a crime in New Jersey.
  5. The waiting period passes. At least 24 hours must pass from the recorded time of death.
  6. The cremation takes place at a crematory, under the state rules described below.
  7. You receive the remains, in a labeled temporary container or in the urn you chose.

If the death is one the county medical examiner must look into, the body stays in the medical examiner's care until it is released. State law lists those deaths. They include accidents, deaths not caused by a readily recognizable disease, and deaths within 24 hours of admission to a hospital or nursing home. That can add time, and the funeral director will keep in touch with the medical examiner's office for you.

Who has the right to authorize a cremation in New Jersey?

The person your parent appointed comes first. If nobody was appointed, New Jersey law sets an order: spouse or partner, then a majority of the adult children, then parents, then a majority of brothers and sisters, then other next of kin.

The law is N.J.S.A. 45:27-22, amended in 2019. A few parts matter a great deal to families:

  • A named "funeral agent." Your parent can appoint someone to control the funeral and disposition in a will, or on a form approved by the New Jersey Cemetery Board, signed in front of at least two witnesses and notarized. The newest valid document wins. The person does not have to be the executor.
  • Siblings decide by majority. When the right falls to the adult children, a majority of them must agree. If you are one of four children, three of you need to sign on.
  • The 72 hour rule. The person or people first in line must act within 72 hours of the death. If they don't, or can't be reached after a reasonable try, the right passes to the next group. A doctor's finding that someone is medically incapacitated also moves it down the line.
  • Divorce ends the right. A former spouse or partner loses the right to decide.
  • No conflicts. An employee or owner of the funeral home, cemetery or crematory can't be the appointed agent unless they are a relative.
  • Anyone can step aside. A person with the right may give it up, and it passes to the next group.

Whoever signs the authorization vouches for the facts on it, including their right to decide, and can be held liable for a false statement. If there is a family disagreement that can't be settled, a court can give other directions. Talk with a lawyer in that case. This page is general information, not legal advice.

If your mom or dad wants cremation, the kindest thing is to put it in writing now and name the person who will carry it out.

That planning fits naturally with a will and power of attorney. Our guide to estate planning in New Jersey covers the rest.

How long do you have to wait before cremation in New Jersey?

At least 24 hours from the time of death on the death certificate. In practice it is often longer, because the death certificate, the permit and the signed authorization all have to be in place first.

The rule comes from N.J.S.A. 26:7-18.1. While your parent waits, state crematory rules require that a body that has not been embalmed and is kept at the crematory for more than 24 hours be refrigerated. If a family member with the right to decide is traveling or hard to reach, tell the funeral director early. The 72 hour clock in the control law still applies.

There is no deadline for a memorial. You can hold one a week or a month later with the urn present, which gives relatives time to travel.

What is the difference between direct cremation and cremation with a service?

Direct cremation happens shortly after death with no embalming, viewing or visitation. Cremation with a service adds a viewing, a funeral, or both before the cremation, which costs more.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) describes direct cremation as the simplest option. The cremated remains go into an urn or other container and can be kept at home, buried, placed in a niche, or scattered. A memorial service can still happen later, at a house of worship, a park or a living room.

With a service first, the funeral home usually prepares the body for viewing, and many homes require embalming for a public viewing. The FTC says no state law requires routine embalming for every death, and you can ask whether a short private family viewing without embalming is possible.

Under the FTC Funeral Rule, a funeral home that offers cremation must tell you that an alternative container is available and must provide one. No state or local law requires a casket for cremation. New Jersey's crematory rules only require that the container be rigid, fully closed, not leaking, and made of materials that won't give off toxic fumes. A crematory can't accept a container made of plastic, fiberglass, Styrofoam, copper or bronze, or one with a zinc liner.

How much does cremation cost in New Jersey?

There is no official New Jersey average. The National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA), a trade group, put the 2023 national median for a funeral with viewing and cremation at $6,280, including the cremation fee, an alternative container and an urn.

That figure leaves out cemetery costs and "cash advance" items the funeral home pays for you, such as flowers or an obituary. Direct cremation skips the embalming, viewing and ceremony charges, so it costs less, though NFDA's release does not give a median for it.

According to the FTC, a direct cremation bill includes the funeral home's basic services fee, transportation and care of the body, and a container or urn. A crematory fee may be included, or added on if the funeral home does not own the crematory. That second case is common here. New Jersey law requires crematories to sit on dedicated cemetery property, except for a few run with funeral homes since before December 1, 1971, so most funeral homes send families to a cemetery-run crematory.

Three questions keep the bill clear:

  • Is the crematory fee included in the direct cremation price, or separate?
  • What container is included, and can we bring our own urn? (The FTC says the funeral home must accept an urn you bought elsewhere, with no handling fee.)
  • How many certified death certificates are included, and what does each extra one cost?

Ask for the General Price List by phone before you visit. Our guide to funeral costs and prepaid funerals in NJ covers your Funeral Rule rights, prepaid plans and help from Social Security in detail. Veterans may qualify for burial benefits; see veterans burial benefits in New Jersey.

What happens at the crematory, and can the family be there?

New Jersey sets detailed rules for crematories so the right person comes back to you. The funeral director has to give the crematory a signed authorization with specific information, and the crematory tracks your parent with a metal identification disc or similar heat-proof tag from arrival to release.

The authorization the funeral director provides must include:

  • Your parent's name, last address, date of birth or age, and the date, time and place of death
  • Whether the death was from an infectious disease, if known
  • A statement that any surgical implants that must come out before cremation have been removed
  • Whether your parent had radiation therapy, what kind and when
  • The name, address, relationship and signature of each person authorizing the cremation

So tell the funeral director about any pacemaker, defibrillator or other implanted device, and about any radiation treatment. They take care of the rest.

At the crematory, staff must identify the remains by at least two separate means the whole time, one of them a metal disc or other tag that survives the heat. Someone must monitor every cremation. Before the remains are removed and again before labeling, staff check the disc against the paperwork. The crematory keeps the authorization form for at least seven years. New Jersey law also says unidentified remains may not be cremated at all.

If you would like to be present when the cremation begins, or to have a short prayer at the crematory, ask the funeral home when you make arrangements. Policies, timing and any fee vary by crematory, so get the answer before the day. Some faiths have their own customs around cremation. Your clergy can tell you what is expected.

What do you get back after a cremation?

You receive the cremated remains, which New Jersey law defines as the bone fragments and container residue left after cremation. They come in a leak-proof container labeled with your parent's name and the date of the cremation.

State rules say metal and other material that doesn't burn is removed. Nothing else may be placed in the container without written instructions from the person who authorized the cremation. The crematory must keep a record of the date of the cremation and who received the remains.

The temporary container is fine for now. You can move the ashes into an urn later, divide them among family members, or keep them in the container until you decide. If you plan to fly with them, choose a container that can be X-rayed, such as wood or plastic. The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) won't open an urn, even if you ask.

When you are ready, our guide to where you can scatter ashes in New Jersey covers the ocean, parks, cemeteries and keeping the urn at home. If you are still working through the paperwork, see what to do when a parent dies. And when the arrangements are done, our list of grief support in NJ is there for you.

Problems with a funeral home go to the State Board of Mortuary Science. Crematories and cemeteries not run by a religious group are overseen by the New Jersey Cemetery Board. Both are part of the Division of Consumer Affairs, 1-800-242-5846.

faq.q: How do I arrange a cremation for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call a funeral home and say you want cremation. The person with the legal right to decide, usually a surviving spouse or a majority of the adult children, signs the authorization. The funeral director handles the death certificate and permit and takes your mom to a crematory. Ask for the General Price List first; funeral homes must give prices by phone.

faq.q: How long after death can a cremation happen in NJ?
faq.a: Not until at least 24 hours have passed from the time of death recorded on the death certificate. It often takes longer because the death certificate, permit and signed authorization must be ready, and longer still if the medical examiner is involved.

faq.q: My siblings and I disagree about cremating our dad. Who decides?
faq.a: If your dad named someone in his will or on the state's notarized form, that person decides. If not, and there is no surviving spouse or partner, a majority of the adult children decides. If you can't reach agreement, a court can give directions, so talk with a lawyer. This is general information, not legal advice.

faq.q: Do we have to buy a casket for cremation?
faq.a: No. The FTC says no state or local law requires a casket for cremation, and a funeral home that offers cremation must make an alternative container available. New Jersey only requires a rigid, closed container that doesn't leak or give off toxic fumes.

faq.q: Is embalming required for cremation in New Jersey?
faq.a: Not for a direct cremation, which has no viewing. Many funeral homes require embalming for a public viewing, so ask about a private family viewing without it if that matters to you.

faq.q: Can I watch the cremation?
faq.a: Ask the funeral home when you make arrangements. Whether family can be present, and whether there is a fee, depends on the crematory, so get an answer ahead of time.

title: Where can you scatter ashes in New Jersey?
dek: The ocean, parks, beaches, private land, cemeteries and home: what the rules say, who to ask, and how to fly or mail ashes.
keyFacts: Ocean scattering must be at least 3 nautical miles from shore, with a report to the EPA within 30 days.
The EPA charges no fee and needs no application before a burial at sea.
Scattering at Sandy Hook (Gateway National Recreation Area) requires a National Park Service permit.
TSA allows ashes in carry-on bags if the container can be X-rayed. Officers won't open an urn.
Since March 1, 2025, USPS requires its Priority Mail Express Cremated Remains box for mailing ashes.
body:
In New Jersey you can scatter ashes at sea, on private land with the owner's permission, or in a cemetery scattering area. You can also bury them, place them in a niche, or keep them at home. Public parks and beaches need permission first, and the Atlantic Ocean has its own federal rule: at least three nautical miles from shore, with a report to the EPA within 30 days.

There is no single New Jersey law that lists where ashes may go. What applies depends on who owns or manages the place. This guide goes through each option your family is likely to consider, with the official rule where one exists and the office to ask where it doesn't.

PlaceWhat you need
Ocean3 nautical miles out; tell EPA in 30 days
Private landThe owner's permission
State parkAsk the park office first
Sandy HookNational park permit
Town beach or parkAsk the town
CemeteryThe cemetery's rules and fees
HomeNothing

Can you scatter ashes in the ocean off New Jersey?

Yes, under a federal general permit from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). You must be at least three nautical miles from land, and you must report the burial to the EPA within 30 days.

A nautical mile is a little longer than a regular mile, so three nautical miles is about 3.5 regular miles. The distance is measured from the low water line, or from a line drawn across the mouth of a bay or river, so the inside of a bay doesn't count as open ocean. Cremated remains can go into water of any depth once you are far enough out.

  • No application in advance. You don't need to ask permission first, and the EPA charges no fee.
  • Report afterward. Use the EPA's online Burial at Sea Reporting Tool, or contact the EPA regional office for the area the boat left from. You don't need to send a death certificate.
  • Use your own boat or hire one. The EPA notes that many charter operators offer burials at sea. For a veteran or a veteran's spouse, the U.S. Navy may be able to arrange one.
  • Containers are allowed if wind makes scattering hard. The container can't have any plastic, can't float, and should break down quickly in seawater.
  • Flowers are fine if they decompose. No plastic flowers, synthetic wreaths, balloons or monuments.
  • Human remains only. You can't mix in a pet's ashes under this permit.
Wading in from the beach doesn't meet the federal rule. Ocean scattering means a boat, three nautical miles out.

If you hire a boat, ask whether the captain files the EPA report or whether you should. Either way, keep a note of the date, the departure point and the location.

Can you scatter ashes in a lake, river or bay in New Jersey?

The federal ocean permit doesn't cover inland waters, and the EPA says states may have their own rules. We did not find a published New Jersey rule on this, so ask before you go.

The EPA suggests contacting the state environmental agency, health agency or mortuary board. In New Jersey, that means the Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP), the Department of Health, or the State Board of Mortuary Science at the Division of Consumer Affairs, 1-800-242-5846. If the lake or river is in a park, the park's own rules also apply.

Can you scatter ashes in a New Jersey state park or on a beach?

Ask first. New Jersey's State Park Service does not publish a scattering policy that we could find, and a national park area in the state requires a permit.

  • State parks and forests. Call the office of the park you have in mind, or the State Park Service at 1-800-843-6420. If you are planning a memorial with a group of people, ask whether you need a Special Use Permit. The State Park Service requires one for organized activities and events and wants the application at least 90 days ahead.
  • Sandy Hook. Sandy Hook is part of Gateway National Recreation Area, run by the National Park Service. Its rules say scattering ashes requires a permit. Federal regulations ban scattering in any national park area except under a permit or in areas the superintendent designates, so check with the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area too if you are thinking of the Gap.
  • Town beaches, parks and boardwalks. These belong to the town or county. Call the municipal clerk or the beach office and ask. Rules can differ from one shore town to the next.

A quiet, private moment is usually what families want anyway. Choose an early morning or off season visit and keep the group small.

Can you scatter ashes on private land?

Yes, with the owner's permission. If the land belongs to someone else, such as the family farm a cousin now owns or a favorite golf course, ask the owner and get the answer in writing.

Think about the future too. If your parent's ashes go into the garden at the family home, they stay there when the house is sold. Some families keep a small portion in a keepsake urn for that reason. Our guide to selling the family home may help if a sale is coming.

What are the cemetery options for ashes in New Jersey?

Cemeteries can bury an urn in a grave, place it in a niche in a columbarium or mausoleum, or offer an area for scattering. Each cemetery sets its own rules and charges, which must be printed and posted.

Under the New Jersey Cemetery Act, a grave can hold cremated remains, and a niche is a space in a columbarium or mausoleum for an urn. The law lets cemeteries adopt reasonable rules and set reasonable charges for niches, products and services, and requires them to post those rules and charges in their offices and on the grounds. Cemeteries must keep a record of every placement of cremated remains.

Questions to ask the cemetery office:

  • Can an urn go into the existing family grave, and who has to give permission?
  • What are the charges to open the grave, place the urn, and add a name to the marker?
  • Does the cemetery require an urn vault or a particular kind of urn?
  • Is there a scattering garden or area, and is a marker or name plaque possible?
  • Do you have columbarium niches, and what do they cost?

Once cremated remains are placed in a grave, removing them later needs the consent of the space's owner and the person with the right to control the remains. Cemeteries that are not run by a religious group are regulated by the New Jersey Cemetery Board, part of the Division of Consumer Affairs. Complaints go to Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846. Eligible veterans and spouses have their own options; see veterans burial benefits in New Jersey.

Cemetery charges are separate from the funeral home's bill. Our guide to funeral costs in NJ explains what the FTC Funeral Rule does and does not cover.

Can you keep ashes at home, travel with them or divide them?

Yes to all three. The Federal Trade Commission notes that cremated remains can be kept in the home, and there are clear federal rules for flying and mailing.

Keeping the urn at home. Many families keep ashes on a shelf for months or years before deciding. There is no deadline. Write down where they are and what your parent wanted, and keep that note with their important papers so the next generation knows.

Flying. The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) allows cremated remains in carry-on and checked bags, but some airlines don't allow them in checked bags, so call your airline. TSA suggests a container made of a lighter material such as wood or plastic. If the X-ray image is opaque, the container won't be allowed through, and TSA officers will not open it, even if you ask. It doesn't hurt to carry a copy of the death certificate or the cremation paperwork.

Mailing. Since March 1, 2025, the U.S. Postal Service requires cremated remains, including keepsakes and jewelry with ashes, to go by Priority Mail Express in its Priority Mail Express Cremated Remains box. Free box kits are available from the online Postal Store.

Taking ashes to another state or country. Check the rules where you are going, especially for scattering. For burial at sea in another country's waters, the EPA says that country's laws apply too.

Dividing ashes. Families often split ashes among siblings, or keep some and scatter the rest. New Jersey's crematory rules say nothing else may be put into the container without written instructions from the person who authorized the cremation, so ask the funeral home before the cremation about several smaller urns or keepsakes. The person with the legal right to control the disposition has the final say. When that right sits with the adult children, a majority must agree, so talk it through together early. Our guide to cremation in New Jersey explains who holds that right.

What if the family can't decide yet?

That's normal. Grief doesn't keep a schedule, and nothing requires you to choose right away.

Keep the ashes in the temporary container until everyone is ready, or place them in a niche for now. Some families wait for an anniversary or a birthday to scatter, or plan a trip to a place your mom or dad loved. If you feel stuck, our list of grief support in NJ includes groups for adult children and spouses. For the paperwork still waiting, see what to do when a parent dies.

This guide is general information, not legal advice.

faq.q: Is it legal to scatter ashes at the Jersey Shore?
faq.a: From the beach, ask the town first, since beaches are run by the municipality, and Sandy Hook needs a National Park Service permit. In the ocean, federal rules require you to be at least three nautical miles from shore and to report the burial to the EPA within 30 days.

faq.q: How do I scatter my dad's ashes at sea?
faq.a: Use your own boat or hire a charter that offers burials at sea, and go at least three nautical miles out. Use only decomposable flowers and no plastic. Within 30 days, report it with the EPA's online Burial at Sea Reporting Tool. If your dad was a veteran, the U.S. Navy may be able to arrange a burial at sea.

faq.q: Can I scatter my mom's ashes in a New Jersey state park?
faq.a: Ask the park office first. We found no published State Park Service policy, so permission is the safe route. For a memorial with a group, ask whether you need a Special Use Permit, which the State Park Service wants at least 90 days ahead. The State Park Service number is 1-800-843-6420.

faq.q: Can we keep ashes at home in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes. Many families keep the urn at home for a while or for good. Write down where the ashes are and what your parent wanted, and keep that note with their important papers.

faq.q: Can I take ashes on a plane?
faq.a: Yes. TSA allows cremated remains in carry-on bags, and in checked bags if your airline allows it. Use a wood or plastic container that shows up clearly on X-ray. TSA officers won't open the container.

faq.q: Can we split the ashes among my siblings?
faq.a: Yes. Ask the funeral home before the cremation about several small urns or keepsakes, and put the instructions in writing. The person with the legal right to control the remains decides; if that is the adult children, a majority must agree.

title: How to find and choose a funeral home in New Jersey
dek: How to look up a funeral home's state license, what to ask on the phone, what to compare on price lists, and the warning signs to watch for.
keyFacts: Every NJ funeral home must be registered with the State Board of Mortuary Science. Check it free on the state's license lookup.
Funeral homes must give prices over the phone, and you don't have to give your name.
In NJ, a body not buried or cremated within 48 hours must be embalmed or refrigerated at 45 degrees or below.
NJ price lists must say if an owner also owns half or more of other NJ funeral homes.
Complaints: Division of Consumer Affairs, 1-800-242-5846 (toll free in NJ).
body:
To find a funeral home in New Jersey, start with two or three homes near where your mom or dad lived, or near where the service will be. Check that each one holds a current registration with the State Board of Mortuary Science, using the state's free license lookup. Then call each home and ask for its prices. Federal law requires every funeral home to give price information over the phone, and you don't have to give your name first.

Most families pick the place they already know, or the one closest to home. That can work out fine. Comparing even two price lists, though, often shows real differences for the same service. A few calls, made by you or a calm friend, can save money and stress.

How do I find funeral homes near my parent?

Make a short list of homes in your parent's town or the next town over, then confirm each one is registered with the state. A funeral home in New Jersey has to be registered with the State Board of Mortuary Science, and the people who run it have to be licensed.

The Division of Consumer Affairs runs the license verification system. It is free and shows current records. Here is how to search it for funeral homes:

  1. Choose Business Search. The state says funeral homes are licensed in the business's name, so they are listed under Business Search.
  2. Pick the profession. Choose "Mortuary Science" as the profession and "Funeral Home" as the license type.
  3. Type the town. Enter at least two letters of the city or town, or part of the funeral home's name. You can leave the other boxes blank.
  4. Open each result. Look at the status and the address. Make sure the address matches the building you plan to use.
  5. Check the director too. Switch to Person Search and look up the funeral director you will work with by name.

The lookup searches by town, not county. If your parent lived near a town line, search the neighboring towns too. The Board also posts its disciplinary actions online. You can call the Board at 973-504-6425 with questions.

There is no government star rating for funeral homes, the way Medicare rates nursing homes. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) suggests searching a funeral home's name online with words like "complaint" or "review," and asking people you trust.

A price list is yours to keep. Ask for it before anyone shows you a casket.

What should I ask when I call a funeral home?

Ask for prices on the exact service you want, and ask what each price includes. Under the FTC Funeral Rule, a funeral home must answer price questions by phone. New Jersey's own rules say the same thing.

The FTC also says many funeral homes will mail, email or text their price lists, though they don't have to. Some post them online. Keep a notepad by the phone and ask the same questions at each home:

  • What is your basic services fee? This is the one charge you can't decline.
  • What does direct cremation cost, and what is included? Is the crematory fee extra?
  • What does immediate burial cost, with and without a family graveside service?
  • What do you charge to bring my parent from the hospital, nursing home or house?
  • What do you charge per day for refrigeration, if we wait for family to arrive?
  • What are your least expensive caskets and alternative containers?
  • Which items are "cash advances" you pay to others, such as death certificates, the obituary or clergy? Do you add a fee to those?
  • Can we bring a casket or urn we bought elsewhere? (The answer has to be yes, with no handling fee.)

If a home won't give prices over the phone, the FTC says to look somewhere else. You can report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

What should I compare on the price lists?

Compare the total for the same set of choices, then look at the biggest line items one by one. Packages can be a good deal, but the FTC says you can only compare fairly by using the itemized General Price List.

Line itemWhat to check
Basic servicesFixed fee; compare it first
TransferPickup fee and any mileage
EmbalmingOnly if you want a viewing
ViewingPrice per day or per hour
Casket or urnLowest priced models
Cash advancesAny markup added

The FTC's basic services fee covers things every funeral needs, such as planning, getting permits and copies of the death certificate, preparing notices, sheltering the body and coordinating with the cemetery or crematory. Cash advances are items the home buys for you from others. A home that adds a fee to them must tell you in writing.

New Jersey adds one useful detail. Each General Price List must say whether any owner of that funeral home also owns half or more of other New Jersey funeral homes, and list them. Two homes with different names may share an owner. The FTC notes that many homes that look locally owned belong to national companies. If that matters to your family, the price list will tell you.

Our guide to funeral costs and prepaid funerals in NJ covers typical prices and your full rights under the Funeral Rule, so we won't repeat them here.

Is embalming required in New Jersey?

No, not for every death. New Jersey's health rules say a body that is not buried or cremated within 48 hours must be embalmed or kept refrigerated at 45 degrees Fahrenheit or below. Refrigeration meets the rule.

The FTC says many funeral homes require embalming for a public viewing, even though the law does not. If you want a viewing but not embalming, ask whether the home offers a short private family viewing instead. Direct cremation and immediate burial need no embalming at all.

A New Jersey funeral director may not take possession of or embalm a body without permission from the person who has the legal right to control the funeral. Under the Funeral Rule, a home also can't charge for embalming you did not approve, unless the law required it. New Jersey's required Statement of Funeral Goods and Services Selected prints that same promise, and must explain in writing any embalming charge.

What are the red flags?

Walk away, or at least slow down, if a funeral home says something the FTC says is false or pushes you to decide today.

  • "The law requires embalming." No state requires routine embalming for every death.
  • "You need a casket for cremation." No state or local law requires one. A home that offers cremation must offer a simple container.
  • "There's a fee to use your casket." The Funeral Rule bans it.
  • "This casket will preserve her." The FTC says no casket or embalming preserves a body forever, and sellers can't claim it.
  • "The vault is required by state law." No state law requires one, though many cemeteries do. Ask the cemetery directly.
  • No written statement. In New Jersey you should get a signed copy of the Statement of Funeral Goods and Services Selected right after you make the arrangements.

Be careful with unexpected calls after a death, too. Scammers read obituaries. Our guide to scams targeting older adults in NJ explains how to check a caller.

How do we handle religious, cultural or out-of-state needs?

Tell each funeral home up front what your family's faith or traditions require, and ask how often they serve families like yours. The State Board of Mortuary Science says its work includes respecting each family's religious values.

Questions worth asking:

  • Can you arrange a burial within a day or two if our faith calls for it?
  • Do you allow ritual washing, a watcher who stays with the body, or family members who help prepare the body?
  • Can the service be held at our house of worship instead of your chapel?
  • Can family members be present at the cremation? (See our cremation guide.)
  • Do you have staff who speak our family's language?

If your parent dies in New Jersey but will be buried in another state, the funeral director files the death certificate here and gets a removal or transit permit. New Jersey law says no one may move a body out of the state without a death certificate and that permit. Often two funeral homes are involved, one to forward your parent and one to receive them. Ask both for their "forwarding remains" and "receiving remains" prices.

If your parent dies in another state and will come home to New Jersey, the death certificate is filed in the state where the death happened. New Jersey's rules don't allow an unembalmed body to be brought into the state more than 48 hours after death, except under a waiver during a declared emergency, so talk to both funeral homes quickly about timing.

Can we switch funeral homes after we've started?

Yes. New Jersey's rules say a funeral director must promptly release a body when the person with the legal right to control the funeral asks. Unless your parent named someone in a will or on the state form, that is the surviving spouse or partner, or if there is none, a majority of the adult children. That person decides which funeral home to use.

Expect to pay the first home for any services it already provided, such as the transfer from the hospital or days of refrigeration. Ask the new home what it charges to receive your parent, and let the two homes coordinate. If a prepaid funeral plan was set up with the first home, New Jersey lets you move it to another home. Our funeral costs guide explains the transfer rules and who has the legal right to decide.

If something goes wrong, file a complaint with the State Board of Mortuary Science through the Division of Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846 (toll free in New Jersey) or 973-504-6200. The funeral home will also handle the death certificate, which you'll need for nearly everything on our list of what to do when a parent dies.

This guide is general information, not legal advice.

faq.q: How do I check if a funeral home is licensed in New Jersey?
faq.a: Use the Division of Consumer Affairs license verification site. Choose Business Search, pick Mortuary Science and Funeral Home, and type the town. To check an individual funeral director, use Person Search. The State Board of Mortuary Science is at 973-504-6425.

faq.q: How do I compare funeral homes for my mom without visiting?
faq.a: Call two or three homes and ask for prices on the same service, such as direct cremation or a viewing and burial. They must answer price questions by phone. Many will also email or text their General Price List, though they don't have to.

faq.q: Does New Jersey require embalming?
faq.a: Not for every death. A body that isn't buried or cremated within 48 hours must be embalmed or refrigerated at 45 degrees Fahrenheit or below. Many funeral homes require embalming for a public viewing, so ask about a private family viewing if you want to skip it.

faq.q: Can I move my dad to a different funeral home?
faq.a: Yes. New Jersey rules require a funeral director to promptly release a body when the person with the legal right to control the funeral asks. You will likely pay the first home for anything it already did, such as the transfer and refrigeration.

faq.q: My mother died in New Jersey but will be buried in another state. How does that work?
faq.a: A New Jersey funeral director files the death certificate here and gets a removal or transit permit, which state law requires before a body leaves New Jersey. Usually one home forwards your mother and another receives her, so ask both for those prices.

faq.q: Where do I complain about a New Jersey funeral home?
faq.a: File a complaint with the State Board of Mortuary Science through the Division of Consumer Affairs, 1-800-242-5846 (toll free in NJ) or 973-504-6200. Price list problems can also be reported to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

title: How to get a death certificate in New Jersey
dek: Who files it, who can order certified copies, what they cost, how many to get, and how to fix a mistake or a cause of death marked pending.
keyFacts: The funeral director files the death certificate, usually through NJ's Electronic Death Registration System.
The state charges $25 for the first certified copy and $2 for each extra copy ordered at the same time. Local fees vary.
Certified copies go to a spouse or partner, adult child, grandchild, sibling, parent, legal representative or someone with a court order.
Informational certifications leave off the cause of death and Social Security number.
The Trenton walk-in office stopped taking cash on June 18, 2026.
body:
In New Jersey, the funeral director files the death certificate, and you can order your first certified copies through the funeral home. Later copies come from the local registrar in the town where the death happened, or from the state Office of Vital Statistics and Registry in Trenton. The state charges $25 for the first copy and $2 for each extra copy of the same record ordered at the same time.

Only certain people can get a certified copy, the kind with a raised seal that banks and courts accept. An adult child, a spouse or civil union partner, a grandchild, a sibling, a parent and a legal representative all qualify, with ID and proof of the relationship.

Who files the death certificate in New Jersey?

The funeral director in charge does. New Jersey law makes the funeral director responsible for completing and filing the death certificate, usually through the state's online system, the New Jersey Electronic Death Registration System (NJ-EDRS).

Two people supply the facts:

  • The family gives the personal details. The funeral director gets these from the person best able to supply them, often you. Have your parent's Social Security number, date and place of birth and their parents' names handy.
  • A doctor or medical examiner certifies the cause of death. The law gives the attending physician, an advanced practice nurse or the medical examiner up to 24 hours after death is pronounced to sign.

The record is not complete until both parts are signed. The funeral director files it with the local registrar in exchange for a burial or removal permit. State law bars burial, cremation or moving a body out of New Jersey without that permit, so the certificate is filed before burial or cremation.

Check the funeral home's draft carefully. A wrong birth date or a misspelled name is much easier to fix before the record is filed.

If your mom or dad died in another state, that state files and issues the death certificate, even if they lived in New Jersey. Order copies from that state's vital records office.

What's the difference between a certified copy and a certification?

A certified copy is the official version. A certification is an informational copy that won't work for legal or money matters.

Certified copyCertification
Raised sealYesNo
Legal useYesNo
Cause of deathShownLeft off
Social Security no.ShownLeft off
Proof of relationshipRequiredNot required

Certified copies are printed on State of New Jersey safety paper with the raised seal of the office that issued them. The state says certifications are generally only useful for family history. For banks, insurers, pensions, the County Surrogate and real estate, order certified copies.

A New Jersey copy from a local registrar is valid for the same purposes as one from Trenton, with one exception. If a foreign government needs the record with an apostille seal, the copy has to come from the state office.

Who is allowed to order a certified copy?

New Jersey limits certified copies to close family and a few others. You must show you are:

  • The person's spouse or civil union partner, or domestic partner
  • Their child, grandchild or sibling, if you are of legal age
  • Their parent, legal guardian or legal representative
  • A state or federal agency for official purposes
  • Someone with a court order

Proving you are the child. The state says that for a parent's record you must send, at minimum, a copy of your own birth certificate showing that parent. If your last name changed when you married, add a copy of your marriage certificate so your ID links to your birth name. A grandchild needs papers linking each generation.

Your ID. Send a copy of a current photo driver's license or non-driver ID showing your current address. Without one, the state accepts two other documents with your current address, such as a recent utility bill or bank statement. Copies are mailed only to the address on your ID unless you include a notarized letter. If you don't drive anymore, see our guide to getting a New Jersey non-driver ID.

Other family members. An ex-spouse can get the record only on behalf of a minor child of the marriage. An attorney can order only for a client who qualifies. If a qualifying relative can't make the trip, they can give you a notarized letter to pick up the copies they applied for.

How do I order copies, and what do they cost?

You have four ways to order. The fastest is in person, either at the local registrar in the town where your parent died or at the state's walk-in office in Trenton.

  1. Through the funeral home. When you make arrangements, tell the funeral director how many copies you want. New Jersey's required Statement of Funeral Goods and Services Selected lists death certificate copies as a cash disbursement, so you'll see the count and price on it.
  2. From the local registrar. Call the vital records office in the municipality where the death happened. Many offer same day service in person. Fees vary by town, so ask before you go.
  3. In person in Trenton. The Office of Vital Statistics and Registry is at 140 East Front Street, open 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays except state holidays. Arrive by 3:30 p.m. to leave with your copy the same day, which can take up to two hours. The office stopped taking cash on June 18, 2026.
  4. By mail. Send form REG-27a with copies of your ID and proof of relationship to NJ Department of Health, Vital Statistics and Registry, P.O. Box 370, Trenton, NJ 08625-0370. Pay by check or money order to "Treasurer, State of New Jersey." Don't mail cash.
  5. Online or by phone through VitalChek. The state's online ordering partner is VitalChek, reachable at 1-877-622-7549. You'll need a credit card and scans of your ID and proof of relationship. VitalChek adds its own processing fee, and faster processing is available for an extra charge.

The state charges $25 for the search and first copy and $2 for each additional copy of the same record ordered at the same time. That makes ordering several at once much cheaper than ordering one at a time.

Expect to wait weeks, not days, for an online or mail order. The state's own pages give different estimates, from about 4 to 8 weeks for online orders and up to 8 to 10 weeks for mail orders, not counting delivery. The state says times vary with the number of requests, so if you need copies quickly, go in person. To check on a mailed request, call 1-866-649-8726. For an online order, call 1-866-628-9244.

The state holds death records from 1951 on. Older ones are at the New Jersey State Archives.

How many copies should we order?

Most families need more certified copies than they expect. Make a list of every place your parent had money, property or benefits, and count one copy for each place that wants an original with a raised seal.

Common places that ask for a certified copy:

  • The County Surrogate, to probate the will or open the estate
  • Each bank, brokerage and retirement account
  • Each life insurance company
  • Pension plans and annuities

Before you mail an original, ask whether a photocopy will do and whether they will send the original back. Usually the funeral home reports the death to Social Security, so you may not need a copy for that. Our list of Social Security offices in NJ has contact details if you need help.

Keep the copies together with your parent's important papers. Our checklist of what to do when a parent dies walks through each call in order.

What if the cause of death says "pending"?

When a medical examiner is investigating, the death certificate can be issued with the cause and manner of death marked "pending" while the investigation and any tests are finished.

New Jersey's medical examiners look into sudden, unexpected or violent deaths. The state's list includes deaths from accidents, deaths after a fall, deaths within 24 hours of surgery and deaths outside a hospital or medical facility, with some exceptions. When the medical examiner takes a case, the medical examiner, not the family doctor, certifies the cause of death.

When the medical examiner finishes, the record is amended with the final cause. Ask the funeral director or the medical examiner's office when to expect it, and ask each insurer or bank whether it will accept a pending copy in the meantime. Then order new certified copies. The state won't replace copies issued before a change. The Office of the Chief State Medical Examiner takes questions at 609-376-0557.

How do I correct a mistake on a death certificate?

File an amendment with the local registrar in the town where the death happened, or with the state on form REG-15 (Application to Amend a Vital Record). Send proof of the correct information, such as a birth or marriage record.

  • Personal details like a name, birth date or parents' names can be corrected with documents that show the right information.
  • Medical details, including the date or place of death and the cause, can only be amended by the doctor who signed the certificate or the medical examiner. The one exception is that the funeral director may correct the place of death for a death at home.
  • Marital status changes that weren't a funeral home typo need proof. The state gives the person who first supplied the information at least 30 days to respond before it accepts the change.

Mail REG-15 to Vital Statistics and Registry, Attention: Vital Record Modifications Unit, P.O. Box 370, Trenton, NJ 08625-0370. Amendments aren't handled at the walk-in counter. For help, call 1-866-649-8726 and choose option 4, or call 609-292-4087. Once the record is fixed, order new certified copies, since earlier copies won't be replaced.

If you're still choosing a funeral home, our guide to choosing a funeral home in New Jersey explains what to ask, and estate planning basics covers what the executor does next. When the paperwork eases, our guide to grief support in NJ may help.

This guide is general information, not legal advice.

faq.q: How do I get a copy of my mom's death certificate in New Jersey?
faq.a: Ask the funeral home to order copies when you make arrangements. Later, order from the local registrar in the town where she died, or from the state Office of Vital Statistics and Registry in person, by mail with form REG-27a, or online through VitalChek. Send ID and a copy of your birth certificate showing her as your parent.

faq.q: How much is a death certificate in New Jersey?
faq.a: The state charges $25 for the first certified copy and $2 for each extra copy of the same record ordered at the same time. Local registrars set their own fees, and VitalChek adds a processing fee for online and phone orders.

faq.q: How long does it take to get a death certificate in NJ?
faq.a: In person, often the same day at the local registrar or the Trenton walk-in office. Online and mail orders take weeks. The state's pages give estimates ranging from about 4 to 8 weeks online and up to 8 to 10 weeks by mail, and say times vary with demand.

faq.q: Can I get my father's death certificate if I'm his stepchild?
faq.a: Stepchildren aren't on the state's list for certified copies, so usually not, unless you have a court order or are the legal representative of the estate. Anyone can request an informational certification, which leaves off the cause of death and Social Security number and can't be used for legal purposes.

faq.q: How many death certificates do I need when a parent dies?
faq.a: Count one certified copy for each place that wants an original: the County Surrogate, each bank and investment account, each life insurer, pensions, and the house or car title. Extra copies ordered at the same time cost $2 each from the state.

faq.q: How do I fix a mistake on a New Jersey death certificate?
faq.a: File form REG-15 with the state, or an amendment with the local registrar, along with proof of the correct information. Only the doctor who signed or the medical examiner can change medical details. Call 1-866-649-8726, option 4, for help.
