title: Veterans burial benefits in New Jersey: a family guide
dek: How to arrange a free burial at Doyle Veterans Cemetery, claim the VA burial allowance, and get a headstone, flag and military honors for your mom or dad.
keyFacts: Burial at Doyle Veterans Cemetery in Burlington County is free for eligible veterans and family. Call 609-738-2400.
VA burial allowance for a non-service-connected death on or after Oct. 1, 2026: up to $1,032, plus $1,032 for a plot.
For a service-connected death on or after Sept. 11, 2001, the VA pays up to $2,000.
Government headstones, markers, medallions, burial flags and military funeral honors are free.
Free help from a county Veterans Service Office: 844-671-1019.
body:
Most veterans who left the military under conditions other than dishonorable can get burial benefits at no cost to the family. In New Jersey that usually means a free grave at the state's veterans cemetery in Burlington County, a government headstone or medallion for a private cemetery, a burial flag, military funeral honors and, in some cases, money from the VA toward the funeral and plot.

The funeral home does much of the work, but only if someone tells it your mom or dad served. Find the DD-214 (the discharge paper) early, because almost every benefit on this page starts with it. This guide is general information, not legal advice.

What burial benefits can a veteran get in New Jersey?

Burial benefits come from two places. The state runs one veterans cemetery, and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) provides markers, flags, certificates and some cash allowances.

BenefitCost to family
Grave at Doyle Veterans CemeteryFree
Headstone, marker or medallionFree; private cemetery setting fees extra
Burial flagFree
Military funeral honorsFree
Presidential Memorial CertificateFree
VA burial and plot allowancePaid to the family if eligible

A spouse can usually be buried with the veteran at a veterans cemetery, even if the spouse dies first. The veteran's service is what counts. Our broader guide to benefits for older veterans in New Jersey covers pensions, tax breaks and health care while your parent is living.

How does burial at Doyle Veterans Cemetery work?

The Brigadier General William C. Doyle Veterans Memorial Cemetery is New Jersey's state veterans cemetery. Burial there is free for eligible veterans and family members, and the funeral director requests the burial at the time of death.

The cemetery covers 225 acres in the Arneytown section of North Hanover Township, about 15 miles southeast of Trenton. The mailing address is 350 Provinceline Road, Wrightstown, NJ 08562. Call 609-738-2400 for general information and interments. The office is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m., except state holidays.

Who is eligible. The cemetery accepts veterans whose last active service ended under other than dishonorable conditions, service members who die on active duty, and certain reservists, including those with 20 years of service creditable for retired pay. Eligible dependents include a spouse, unmarried children under 21 and adult children who could not support themselves because of a disability that began before 21.

New Jersey residency. State rules add a residency test. The person being buried, whether the veteran or a family member, must have been a legal resident of New Jersey at death or have lived at least half of their life in the state. A New Jersey driver's license, voter registration card, paid property tax bill, deed or a utility bill from the last 90 days can serve as proof. If your parent moved away late in life, call the cemetery before you make plans.

What is free. The cemetery does not charge for the grave, its upkeep, a government headstone or niche cover, or a concrete grave liner. A family can buy a private vault instead of the liner, which must be arranged in advance. The family still pays the funeral home to prepare and transport the body or ashes.

  1. Choose a funeral home. Tell the funeral director your parent was a veteran and you would like Doyle. Our guide to choosing a funeral home explains what to compare.
  2. Gather proof of service. A DD-214 works. Older forms such as WD AGO 53 (Army) or NAVPERS 553 (Navy) also work. Retired reservists need a document showing active service other than training. Have proof of New Jersey residency ready too.
  3. The funeral director calls the cemetery while you are there, and faxes the papers to 609-758-0169. Burial is scheduled only after eligibility is confirmed. If papers are missing, the cemetery can help, but checking can take up to five business days.
  4. Plan the day. Services are held on business days between 9:30 a.m. and 3 p.m. They are short and held at a chapel or committal shelter, not at the grave.

Graves and columbarium niches cannot be reserved. The grave is assigned the afternoon before the burial, and the cemetery will try to place your parent near a relative already buried there if you ask.

Cremated remains. A family can arrange an urn burial directly with the cemetery, without a funeral home. Bring the ashes, the cremation certificate and the death certificate on the day. The plastic container most crematories use is fine for burial. Our guide to cremation in New Jersey explains how cremation works.

Find the DD-214 before you need it. Nearly every veteran burial benefit starts there.

Are there national cemeteries in New Jersey?

Yes, two, but both have limited space. Washington Crossing National Cemetery, just across the Delaware River in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, manages both and has open space.

  • Beverly National Cemetery in Burlington County is closed to new burials. It accepts a veteran or eligible family member into a gravesite that already holds a relative.
  • Finn's Point National Cemetery near Salem, in Salem County, has space for cremated remains. Casketed remains may fit only in the same gravesite as a family member already buried there.
  • Washington Crossing National Cemetery in Newtown, Pennsylvania, has space for caskets and cremated remains. It also manages Beverly and Finn's Point.

Burial in a VA national cemetery is scheduled through the National Cemetery Scheduling Office, not the cemetery itself. You or the funeral director fax discharge papers to 866-900-6417, then call 800-535-1117 (weekdays 8 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Eastern). National cemeteries hold burials Monday through Friday.

How much does the VA pay toward a veteran's funeral?

For a death that is not service connected on or after October 1, 2026, the VA pays up to $1,032 toward burial and $1,032 toward a plot. For a service-connected death on or after September 11, 2001, the most it pays is $2,000.

The non-service-connected allowance is not automatic for every veteran. One of these must be true:

  • Your parent was getting VA pension or disability compensation, or would have been if not for military retirement pay.
  • Your parent died in VA care, at a VA facility or one under VA contract.
  • Your parent had a VA compensation or pension claim pending and would have been entitled to it.
  • Your parent died while traveling to or from VA-authorized care.

Whoever paid the funeral bills can apply, as long as no one else will reimburse them. That can be a spouse, a child, a parent, the executor, a friend or a funeral home. Apply online at VA.gov or mail VA Form 21P-530EZ to the Pension Intake Center, PO Box 5365, Janesville, WI 53547-5365. Include the death certificate showing the cause of death, and a copy of the DD-214 helps.

Deadlines. There is no deadline for a service-connected death. For a death that is not service connected, the burial allowance claim is due within 2 years of the burial. There is no deadline for the plot allowance, for transportation costs, or when the veteran died in VA care.

A surviving spouse may not need to file. The VA says if your mom is listed as the veteran's spouse in the VA's records, it automatically pays a set amount to her when it learns of the death.

If the veteran is buried in a VA national cemetery, the VA may also repay the cost of moving the remains there. Keep receipts in your own name. Our guide to funeral costs and prepaid funerals covers what the rest of the bill usually looks like.

How do we get a headstone or medallion for a private cemetery?

The VA provides a government headstone or marker free for an eligible veteran's unmarked grave in any cemetery. If the family already bought a private headstone, the VA can send a bronze medallion to attach to it instead.

At Doyle and at national cemeteries, cemetery staff order the marker for you. At a private cemetery, the family or funeral home applies:

  • Headstone or flat marker: VA Form 40-1330. Upright headstones come in granite and marble, flat markers in granite, marble and bronze. The private cemetery must allow the style you choose, and it can charge you to set it.
  • Medallion: VA Form 40-1330M, for a veteran buried in a private cemetery with a privately purchased headstone. A representative of the cemetery must review and sign the form.
  • Urn or plaque: If your dad was cremated and his ashes were not buried or placed in a columbarium, VA Form 40-1330UP requests a commemorative urn or plaque. Choosing one means he can no longer be buried in a VA national cemetery or get a government headstone later, so think it over first.

Mail forms with a copy of the DD-214 to NCA FP Evidence Intake Center, PO Box 5237, Janesville, WI 53547, or upload them with the VA's QuickSubmit tool. Questions go to 800-697-6947, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern.

How do we arrange military funeral honors and a burial flag?

Ask the funeral director. Funeral directors usually request military funeral honors and the burial flag for the family, and both are free.

New Jersey's Department of Veterans Affairs says every honorably discharged veteran is entitled to basic honors. That means a detail of two or three service members, the playing of Taps, and the folding and presenting of the flag to the next of kin. Military retirees can get a larger detail with a firing party. At Doyle, honors for most veterans are two military representatives who present the flag, with Taps played electronically.

  • Army burials in New Jersey: requests go to the Casualty Assistance Center at Fort Dix, 609-562-4453.
  • Other branches: the funeral director uses the Defense Department's Military Funeral Honors directory. If your dad served in more than one branch, contact the last one.
  • Burial flag: fill out VA Form 27-2008 and bring it to the funeral director, a VA regional office or a post office that keeps flags. Only one flag is issued per veteran, and the VA cannot replace a lost one.
  • Presidential Memorial Certificate: a printed certificate signed by the current president. Families get one automatically at a national cemetery burial. Otherwise apply with VA Form 40-0247. The VA accepts more than one request, so siblings can each have a copy.

Can my dad find out now if he is eligible?

Yes. Checking ahead of time saves your family a stressful search for papers in the first days after a death.

For a VA national cemetery, apply for a pre-need determination of eligibility online or with VA Form 40-10007. Mail it to NCA Evidence Intake Center, PO Box 5237, Janesville, WI 53547, or fax it to the scheduling office. The decision letter does not reserve a grave, but at the time of death the funeral director can call and schedule.

For Doyle, the VA program does not apply. Use the cemetery's own pre-registration form instead. Bring it to the cemetery or any county Veterans Service Office, or mail it with a copy of the DD-214. Pre-registration is not a reserved grave, but it heads off delays.

If you cannot find the DD-214, a child, sibling, parent or unremarried spouse can request it from the National Archives with Standard Form 180 and proof of death. New Jersey's Department of Veterans Affairs also keeps copies of many active duty DD-214s from the 1980s on, for service members whose home of record was New Jersey. Email a signed SF-180 in PDF form to MilRecords@dva.nj.gov or call 609-530-6823. For a military funeral, the funeral director can make the request as next of kin. If your parent is being buried in a national cemetery, the scheduling office will try to find the records for you. Keep the DD-214 with your parent's important papers.

Free help in every county

The state runs a Veterans Service Office in all 21 counties. Accredited officers help with burial allowances, headstones and survivor benefits at no charge. Call 844-671-1019. In Essex County the office is at the VA Newark Regional Office, 20 Washington Place, Newark.

When the funeral is behind you, our guides to what to do when a parent dies, getting death certificates and grief support cover the next steps.

faq.q: How do I get my dad buried at the veterans cemetery in New Jersey?
faq.a: Choose a funeral home and tell them you want Doyle Veterans Cemetery in Burlington County. The funeral director calls the cemetery at 609-738-2400 and faxes his DD-214. Burial is scheduled once eligibility is confirmed. He must have been a New Jersey resident at death or have lived at least half his life in the state. Graves cannot be reserved ahead of time.

faq.q: Can my mom be buried with my dad at Doyle if she was not a veteran?
faq.a: Yes. A veteran's spouse is eligible for burial at Doyle, even if she dies first. In that case the veteran signs a statement agreeing to be buried in the same grave later. A surviving spouse who remarried a non-veteran and died on or after January 1, 2000, is still eligible.

faq.q: Is the VA burial allowance automatic?
faq.a: Not usually. Whoever paid for the funeral applies online or with VA Form 21P-530EZ. One exception: if the surviving spouse is listed in the VA's records, the VA says it pays a set amount to her automatically when it learns of the death.

faq.q: Does a veteran get a free headstone in a private cemetery?
faq.a: Yes, if the grave is unmarked. Apply with VA Form 40-1330. If the family already bought a headstone, request a bronze medallion with VA Form 40-1330M. The marker is free, but the private cemetery may charge to set it.

faq.q: How do I request military funeral honors for my father?
faq.a: Ask the funeral director, who usually handles it. Have his DD-214 or other proof of honorable service ready. For Army burials in New Jersey, requests go to the Casualty Assistance Center at Fort Dix, 609-562-4453.

faq.q: What if we cannot find the DD-214?
faq.a: Next of kin can request it from the National Archives with Standard Form 180 and proof of death. New Jersey's Department of Veterans Affairs also holds many DD-214s for New Jersey service members discharged since the 1980s and a funeral director can request one for a military funeral. Call 609-530-6823.

title: Funeral homes and cemeteries in Essex County, NJ
dek: How to find and check a licensed funeral home in any Essex town, the larger nonsectarian cemeteries, the medical examiner, veterans help and county aid when money is short.
keyFacts: Check any funeral home in the state's free license lookup under Mortuary Science, by town.
Northern Regional Medical Examiner (covers Essex): 862-350-5000, 24-hour line 973-648-4500.
Essex County Veterans Service Office: 609-671-3536, or 844-671-1019 statewide.
Public funeral aid for eligible adults: up to $3,056 funeral and $714 cemetery or crematory.
Essex Division of Family Assistance and Benefits: 973-395-8000.
body:
To find a funeral home in Essex County, start with the state's free license lookup. Every funeral home in New Jersey must be registered with the State Board of Mortuary Science, and the lookup lets you search registered funeral homes by town, from Newark and Montclair to Livingston and the Caldwells. Call two or three, ask for prices over the phone, and compare.

This page covers the local side of a death in Essex County: checking a funeral home, the larger nonprofit cemeteries, when the regional medical examiner gets involved, where death certificates come from, help for veterans, and county help when a family cannot pay. It is general information, not legal advice.

How do I find a licensed funeral home in Essex County?

Use the state's license lookup and search by town. It shows only registered businesses, so it is the safest place to start.

  1. Open the business search. Go to the New Jersey License Verification business search, run by the Division of Consumer Affairs.
  2. Pick the profession. Choose Mortuary Science from the Profession list.
  3. Type the town. Enter at least the first two letters of the city, such as Montclair, Nutley or West Orange, and search. Try the neighboring towns too, since many families use a funeral home a few miles away.
  4. Open each result. Check that the registration is current. To check the individual funeral director, switch to the person search and enter their last name.

Once you have two or three names, call each one. Under the Federal Trade Commission's Funeral Rule, a funeral home must give you prices over the phone, and you do not have to give your name first. Our guide to choosing a funeral home in New Jersey has the questions to ask, and our guide to funeral costs and prepaid funerals explains the price list line by line.

Ask for the price list by phone before you visit. It is your right.

Say your mom lived in Bloomfield and the family now lives in Verona and Cedar Grove. Search all three towns, then pick the funeral home that is easiest for the people who will visit. The location of the funeral home does not have to match where she lived.

If you have a question about a funeral home or want to file a complaint, call the State Board of Mortuary Science at 973-504-6425 or the Division of Consumer Affairs hotline at 973-504-6200 (800-242-5846 toll free in New Jersey).

Where are funeral homes in Essex County?

There are funeral homes in almost every Essex town. Below is a small sample in a few towns, to help you get started. The state license lookup above has the full list.

We checked these listings in November 2026. This is not an endorsement or a ranking. We list a funeral home only when a town or county government page names it and its own website confirms the town and phone number. Phone numbers come from each funeral home's website.

Newark, the Oranges, West Orange, Belleville, Millburn, Cedar Grove and other towns have funeral homes too. We just could not confirm them the same way, so search those towns in the state lookup. Before you sign anything, look up the funeral home there and check that its registration is current.

Which cemeteries are in Essex County?

Essex has large historic cemeteries in Newark and Montclair, plus many religious and church cemeteries. The two below are nonsectarian, which means they serve families of any faith.

We checked these listings in November 2026. They are listed alphabetically. This is not an endorsement or a ranking.

CemeteryTownPhone
Fairmount CemeteryNewark973-623-0695
Rosedale CemeteryMontclair973-673-0127
  • Fairmount Cemetery is at 620 Central Avenue in Newark. Its website lists in-ground burial, cremation services and mausoleum space, and says a new mausoleum is planned.
  • Rosedale Cemetery has its entrance at 408 Orange Road in Montclair. It has a crematory on its grounds, columbarium niches for urns, and a hilltop scattering garden set aside for ashes. Its office is open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Saturday 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. and Sunday 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

Prices for graves and services vary a lot from one cemetery to the next. Cemeteries regulated by the New Jersey Cemetery Board must post their price list in the office and file it with the board. The board does not set prices, but it will send you a copy of a cemetery's filed fees if you call 973-504-6553.

The Cemetery Board regulates only nonsectarian cemetery companies. Catholic cemeteries in the Archdiocese of Newark are run by the archdiocese's Catholic Cemeteries office. Jewish cemeteries and church burial grounds usually have their own offices or work through a congregation, so ask your parent's house of worship. If you cannot find where a relative is buried, the board suggests calling the state's Vital Statistics office at 609-292-4087.

For a parent who served in the military, burial at the state's Brigadier General William C. Doyle Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Wrightstown is free for eligible veterans unless the family chooses its own vault. See our guide to veterans burial benefits.

When does the medical examiner get involved in Essex County?

The Northern Regional Medical Examiner's Office in Newark handles reportable deaths in Essex, Hudson, Passaic, Somerset and Union counties. Its investigators work around the clock.

The state lists the kinds of deaths that must be reported. They include:

  • Deaths outside a hospital or medical facility
  • Deaths in a hospital or nursing home within 24 hours of arriving
  • Deaths after a fall, before or during a hospital stay
  • Deaths within 24 hours of surgery or a diagnostic procedure
  • Deaths that are violent, suspicious or unusual

The fall rule matters for many families of older adults. If your dad fell at home, went to the hospital and died later, the medical examiner may review the case even though he was in the hospital for days. The review can delay the funeral, and a cremation usually waits until the case is released. The funeral home will usually stay in touch with the office for you.

The office's main number is 862-350-5000, and its 24-hour line is 973-648-4500. If your parent was in hospice, ask the hospice team what will happen when the death occurs, so the family knows who to call first.

Where do I get a death certificate in Essex County?

Certified copies come from the local registrar in the town where the death happened, not where your parent lived. If your mom lived in Maplewood but died at a hospital in Livingston, you would order from Livingston.

Most families order their first copies through the funeral home, which adds them to the bill. You can order more later from the town or from the state's Office of Vital Statistics and Registry. Our guide to getting a death certificate in New Jersey covers who can order, the fees and how many copies you are likely to need.

What help is there for veterans and their families in Essex County?

The New Jersey Department of Military and Veterans Affairs runs free Veterans Service Offices that help families apply for burial benefits, headstones and survivor benefits.

OfficeWherePhone
Essex County VSO20 Washington Place, Newark609-671-3536
Newark City Hall920 Broad St., Room B-3973-424-1968
Statewide lineAny county844-671-1019

The Essex office is in the VA Newark Regional Office, fourth floor, Room 439, and is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., closed alternate Fridays. The Newark City Hall office is open Monday to Thursday. There are also set hours at the East Orange VA Medical Center, so call before you go. Bring your parent's discharge papers (DD-214) if you have them.

What if the family cannot pay for a funeral in Essex County?

New Jersey can help pay for a funeral and burial or cremation when the person who died was getting certain public benefits. In Essex County, the place to call is the Division of Family Assistance and Benefits.

Under the state's Work First New Jersey rules, claims can be considered for people who were receiving Work First New Jersey cash assistance, General Assistance, Supplemental Security Income (SSI) or Medicaid Only at the time of death, and for several other groups, such as Medicaid nursing home residents. The rules set these limits for an adult:

AllowanceUp to
Funeral home$3,056
Cemetery or crematory$714
Family can add$1,570

The family and others may chip in up to $1,570 without it lowering the state's payment. Larger contributions are counted. Any prepaid funeral plan reduces the allowance dollar for dollar. For a cremation, the crematory charge comes out of the cemetery allowance and an urn comes out of the funeral allowance.

Call before the service

The rules say the family or funeral home should notify the county agency before the funeral takes place, so the claim can be discussed. Tell the funeral director right away that you plan to ask for public help. The funeral home then has 30 days after the burial or cremation to file its petition.

Essex County Department of Citizen Services, Division of Family Assistance and Benefits, is at 320 University Avenue, second floor, Newark. Call 973-395-8000. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, with the last appointment at 3 p.m.

State law also lets cemeteries join a Cemetery Board registry of companies that accept these public payments as payment in full. Ask the Cemetery Board for the current list at 973-504-6553. Some public burials fall outside these rules, so if your relative was not on any benefits and there is no money at all, ask the county agency or your town's social services office what applies.

For other ways to bring the cost down, such as direct cremation or a memorial service later, see our cremation guide and our guide to crematories in North Jersey. For the bigger checklist after a death, start with what to do when a parent dies, and find more local help on our Essex County page.

faq.q: How do I find a funeral home near my mom in Essex County?
faq.a: Use the free New Jersey License Verification business search, choose Mortuary Science, and type her town. It lists only registered funeral homes. Search nearby towns too, then call two or three and ask for prices by phone.

faq.q: How do I check that a New Jersey funeral home is licensed?
faq.a: Search the funeral home by town in the state's license lookup under Mortuary Science, and check that the registration is current. You can also search the funeral director by last name. Questions go to the State Board of Mortuary Science at 973-504-6425.

faq.q: Which medical examiner covers Essex County?
faq.a: The Northern Regional Medical Examiner's Office in Newark, which also covers Hudson, Passaic, Somerset and Union counties. Its main number is 862-350-5000 and its 24-hour line is 973-648-4500.

faq.q: Does Essex County help pay for funerals?
faq.a: If the person who died was on benefits such as SSI, General Assistance, Work First New Jersey or Medicaid Only, the state's rules allow up to $3,056 for the funeral home and $714 for the cemetery or crematory for an adult. Call the Essex County Division of Family Assistance and Benefits at 973-395-8000 before the service.

faq.q: My dad was a veteran. Who can help us in Essex County?
faq.a: The state's Essex County Veterans Service Office at the VA Newark Regional Office, 20 Washington Place, helps families apply for burial benefits and markers for free. Call 609-671-3536 or the statewide line at 844-671-1019.

faq.q: Does the Cemetery Board regulate every cemetery in Essex County?
faq.a: No. It regulates nonsectarian cemetery companies. Religious cemeteries, such as Catholic and many Jewish cemeteries, are run by their own offices. The board's number is 973-504-6553.

title: Crematories in North Jersey: a guide for NJ families
dek: How cremation works through a North Jersey funeral home, the crematories we could confirm, witnessing, timing, and where ashes can go close to home.
keyFacts: New Jersey law bars cremation until at least 24 hours after the time of death on the death certificate.
New Jersey crematories sit on cemetery grounds, apart from some older funeral home crematories.
Ashes may go in the ocean only 3 or more nautical miles out. Tell the EPA within 30 days.
New Jersey Cemetery Board: 973-504-6553.
Public aid can cover a crematory charge from a cemetery allowance of up to $714 for an adult.
body:
In North Jersey, most families arrange a cremation through a funeral home, and the funeral home brings your loved one to a crematory. Under current New Jersey law, crematories sit on cemetery grounds, apart from some older crematories run with funeral homes, so the crematory is often part of a local cemetery. You can ask the funeral home which one it uses, and in many cases you can visit or even watch the cremation begin.

This page lists crematories in North Jersey that we could confirm, explains how timing works, and covers where ashes can go close to home. It is general information, not legal advice. For the full picture of how cremation works, start with our guide to cremation in New Jersey.

Do I need a funeral home to arrange a cremation in New Jersey?

In practice, almost every family uses one. The funeral home usually brings your parent into its care, works with the doctor or medical examiner on the death certificate, gets the permit and handles transport to the crematory.

New Jersey law makes it illegal to cremate a body without first getting a permit for burial or other final disposition. It also says no one may cremate a body until at least 24 hours have passed since the time of death on the death certificate. Those two rules shape the schedule.

The person with the legal right to make the decision signs the cremation authorization. That is usually the person your parent named in a will or on the state form for a funeral agent, then the spouse, then a majority of the adult children. Our cremation guide walks through the full order.

If you have not picked a funeral home yet, our guide to choosing a funeral home in New Jersey explains how to compare them, and our Essex County page shows how to search the state license lookup by town.

Which crematories are in North Jersey?

We looked at Essex, Bergen, Hudson, Passaic, Morris and Union counties. We list a crematory only when we could confirm it on an official source, such as state Cemetery Board records or a state environmental permit, and on its own website. Phone numbers come from each crematory's own site.

We checked these listings in November 2026. They are grouped by county and listed alphabetically. This is not an endorsement or a ranking.

CrematoryTownPhone
Essex County
Rosedale CemeteryMontclair973-673-0127
Union County
Evergreen Cemetery & CrematoryHillside908-352-7940
Rosehill Crematory & ColumbariumLinden908-862-3902
  • Rosedale Cemetery, entrance at 408 Orange Road, Montclair. Crematory, columbarium, a witnessing room, a chapel and a scattering garden.
  • Evergreen Cemetery & Crematory, 1137 North Broad Street, Hillside. Its website says it has run a crematory on its grounds since the 1970s and offers columbarium niches, urn burial and scattering on the grounds.
  • Rosehill Crematory & Columbarium, 792 East Edgar Road, Linden, run by Rosedale & Rosehill Cemetery. The crematory office is open weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and Saturday 8 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.

We could not confirm a crematory in Bergen, Hudson, Passaic or Morris County on both an official source and the crematory's own website, so none is listed there. That does not mean there are none. Your funeral home will know which crematories it works with, and the New Jersey Cemetery Board can answer questions at 973-504-6553.

You can ask exactly where your mom will be cremated, and when.

How do I find out which crematory a funeral home uses?

Ask. A good funeral home will tell you the name and town of the crematory without hesitation. Questions worth asking on the phone:

  • Which crematory do you use, and who owns it?
  • How is my mom identified from the time you pick her up until the ashes come back?
  • Can our family see her before the cremation, or be there when it starts?
  • Is the crematory fee included in your direct cremation price, or added separately?
  • When will the ashes be ready, and what container will they come in?

The Federal Trade Commission's Funeral Rule protects you here. A funeral home must give you prices by phone. A funeral home that offers cremation must tell you that an alternative container, such as unfinished wood or cardboard, is available instead of a casket, because no law requires a casket for cremation. If the funeral home says the crematory requires you to buy something, it must explain that requirement in writing. You may also bring an urn you bought elsewhere, and the funeral home cannot charge you to use it.

Can our family witness a cremation in North Jersey?

Often, yes. Some families want to be there, and in some faiths a family member starts the cremation.

Rosedale Cemetery in Montclair, for example, has a private witnessing room so families can watch the start of the cremation, and a chapel for final prayers or a short viewing. Other crematories have their own rooms and rules. Tell the funeral home early that you want to witness, because it has to book a time with the crematory. Ask whether it changes the price.

Say your dad wanted a short prayer before cremation and your brother is flying in from Florida. Ask the funeral home to schedule the cremation for the day after he lands, with a half hour in the crematory's chapel. The 24-hour legal wait will already have passed, and the family gets a calm goodbye.

How long does cremation take in North Jersey?

The law sets a minimum of 24 hours after the time of death. The real schedule depends on the paperwork, the authorization and whether the medical examiner is involved.

If a death must be reported, for example a death at home or after a fall, the medical examiner reviews it first. In Essex, Hudson, Passaic and Union counties, that is the Northern Regional Medical Examiner's Office in Newark (862-350-5000). The cremation waits until the case is released. If your parent died in Bergen or Morris County, the funeral home will know which medical examiner office handles the case.

Holidays, weekends and family travel can also push the date. Ask the funeral home for a written estimate of when the ashes will be ready, and ask it to call you if anything changes.

Where can ashes go in North Jersey?

You have several choices close to home. You can also keep the ashes at home while the family decides. There is no rush.

  • A cemetery scattering garden. Rosedale in Montclair has a hilltop scattering garden set aside only for ashes. Evergreen in Hillside offers scattering on its grounds.
  • A columbarium niche. Rosedale, Rosehill in Linden and Evergreen all have columbarium space for urns. Catholic cemeteries in the Archdiocese of Newark also offer cremation niches.
  • A family grave. Many cemeteries let you bury an urn in an existing family plot. Ask the cemetery about its rules and its fee for opening the grave.
  • A veterans cemetery. The state's Doyle Veterans Memorial Cemetery in Wrightstown has columbarium niches for eligible veterans. See our guide to veterans burial benefits.
  • The ocean. Under the Environmental Protection Agency's general permit, ashes may be placed in the ocean only at least three nautical miles from shore. You must tell the EPA within 30 days, which you can do with its online Burial at Sea Reporting Tool. Flowers must be the kind that break down in water, not plastic.

Some families divide the ashes so each child can keep a small portion in a keepsake urn, with the rest placed in a niche or scattering garden. If you plan to do this, ask the funeral home to handle the dividing and to label each container, so nothing gets mixed up later. Talk it through as a family first, because a niche or grave is harder to change once the urn is placed.

Rivers, lakes and bays are not covered by the EPA permit, and state rules can apply. For parks, beaches, private land and flying with ashes, see our guide to where you can scatter ashes in New Jersey.

What does cremation cost, and who checks on crematories?

Costs vary by funeral home and crematory, so compare written price lists. Our guide to funeral costs and prepaid funerals has the national median figures and explains each line.

The New Jersey Cemetery Board oversees nonsectarian cemetery companies, including their crematories. It does not set prices. Cemeteries under the board must post their price lists and file them with the board, and the board will send you a copy if you call 973-504-6553. You can also file a complaint with the board.

If your parent was on SSI, General Assistance, Work First New Jersey or Medicaid Only, state rules may help pay. For an adult, the crematory charge comes out of a cemetery allowance of up to $714, and an urn comes out of a funeral allowance of up to $3,056. Tell the funeral home before the service that you plan to apply, and call your county social services office. In Essex County that is 973-395-8000.

When you are ready, our guide to grief support in New Jersey lists groups and counselors for the months ahead.

faq.q: How do I find out where my mom will be cremated?
faq.a: Ask the funeral home for the name and town of the crematory it uses. A funeral home should tell you right away. You can also ask how your mom will be identified from pickup until the ashes are returned.

faq.q: How soon after death can a cremation happen in New Jersey?
faq.a: Not until at least 24 hours after the time of death on the death certificate. A permit for final disposition is also required, and a medical examiner case must be released first, so it often takes longer.

faq.q: Can we watch the cremation?
faq.a: Often, yes. Some North Jersey crematories, such as Rosedale Cemetery in Montclair, have a witnessing room where family can watch the start. Ask the funeral home early so it can book a time, and ask whether it changes the price.

faq.q: Do I need a casket for cremation in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. The FTC says no state or local law requires a casket for cremation. A funeral home that offers cremation must tell you about alternative containers, such as unfinished wood or cardboard, and make them available.

faq.q: Can I scatter my dad's ashes off the Jersey Shore?
faq.a: Yes, if it is at least three nautical miles from shore, under the EPA's burial at sea permit. You must report it to the EPA within 30 days, which you can do online. Use only flowers that break down in water.

faq.q: Who regulates crematories in New Jersey?
faq.a: The New Jersey Cemetery Board oversees nonsectarian cemetery companies and their crematories. It does not set prices, but it can send you a cemetery's filed price list. Call 973-504-6553.

title: Independent living and 55+ communities in New Jersey
dek: How 55+ age rules work, what association fees cover, renting versus buying, and what happens when your parent needs more help.
keyFacts: A 55+ community must keep at least 80% of occupied units with a resident 55 or older (24 CFR 100.305).
Age-restricted communities must update their occupancy surveys at least every two years.
DCA can act on association open meetings, records access and dispute resolution, not fee increases.
Condo owners who pay property taxes on their unit count as homeowners for NJ property tax relief; condo renters count as renters.
DCA Bureau of Homeowner Protection: 609-984-7905.
body:
Independent living is housing for older adults who can still manage on their own but want less upkeep and more company. In New Jersey that usually means one of two things: a 55+ active adult community where your mom or dad buys a home, or a senior apartment community where they rent and pay a monthly fee that bundles meals, housekeeping, transportation and activities.

Neither one is a care setting. Staff do not help with bathing, dressing or medications as part of the deal. If that kind of help is needed, it comes from a home care agency brought in from outside, or from a move to assisted living or a continuing care retirement community. This guide covers how 55+ rules work, what association fees pay for, renting versus buying, and what to check before your parent signs.

What is the difference between independent living and assisted living?

Independent living offers housing and convenience. Assisted living adds hands-on care. The New Jersey Department of Health licenses assisted living residences and nursing homes. An independent living building is set up for people who can live on their own.

The New Jersey Division of Aging Services describes a few kinds of independent housing. Adult retirement communities are built for active, independent older people, with homes that are usually for sale and sometimes for rent, plus a clubhouse and activities. Congregate apartment housing is a step up in services. It has shared dining, and the state's description says developments offer at least one hot meal a day and some housekeeping.

SettingOwn or rentCare on site
55+ communityUsually ownNo
Senior apartmentsRentNo
CCRCContractYes
Assisted livingRentYes

A good test is to ask whether any part of the building holds a Department of Health license. If it does, look it up in the state's long-term care facility search. If not, you are looking at housing, and any care your parent needs later will be arranged separately. Our overview of senior housing choices compares every setting side by side.

How do 55+ communities work under federal law?

A community can legally turn away families with children only if it meets the federal Housing for Older Persons Act rules. The main test is that at least 80 percent of occupied units have at least one person 55 or older.

The federal Fair Housing Act bans discrimination against families with children, with an exemption for "housing for older persons." There are two common versions. One is housing intended for and occupied only by people 62 and older. The other, far more common in New Jersey, is housing for people 55 and older. To qualify for the 55+ version, a community must do three things under 24 CFR 100.305 to 100.307:

  • Keep at least 80 percent of its occupied units occupied by at least one person 55 or older.
  • Publish and follow policies that show it is meant for people 55 and older.
  • Verify ages, using a driver's license, birth certificate, passport or a signed certification, and update its occupancy survey at least once every two years.

That 80 percent rule leaves room for up to 20 percent of homes to have no one 55 or older. Each community sets its own rule for those units. Some allow a younger spouse or an adult child to live there. Others set a minimum age for every resident. Read the age rules in the governing documents before your parent buys, especially if a younger spouse, partner or caregiver may move in.

New Jersey adds a step on resales. The Department of Community Affairs (DCA) publishes a certification that buyers in an age-restricted community sign, stating the home will be occupied in line with the federal older persons rules. It is recorded with the deed.

The 55+ label is a legal status with rules behind it. Ask to see the age policy in writing.

What do association rules and fees mean for a 55+ home?

Most 55+ communities in New Jersey are run by a homeowners, condominium or cooperative association, and your parent will pay it a monthly fee and live by its rules. The fee typically pays for shared things such as the clubhouse, grounds, and often lawn care and snow removal.

The DCA's Planned Real Estate Development program requires developers of these communities to register an offering plan with the state before selling homes. After the developer leaves, the owners' association is in charge. The DCA's Association Regulation Initiative can step in on only three things:

  • Open meetings. When the board takes a binding vote, owners must get written notice at least 48 hours ahead.
  • Financial records. Owners have a right to inspect the association's accounting records.
  • Dispute resolution. The association must have a written alternative dispute resolution procedure. In a condominium, you must be offered it before a fine is imposed.

DCA says plainly that no government agency oversees property management companies, association elections or maintenance fee increases. That makes your own homework before buying more important. Ask for the budget, the reserve study, the last two years of board minutes and a history of fee increases and special assessments. Ask what the fee covers and what it does not, such as roofs, driveways or interior repairs.

The DCA also warns that if an owner stops paying fees, even over a real dispute, the association can file a lien. In a condominium this can be done without going to court, and the association can foreclose.

Questions about a 55+ community or association

Call the DCA Bureau of Homeowner Protection at 609-984-7905. It handles Planned Real Estate Development, association rules and continuing care retirement communities.

Should your parent rent or buy?

Buying in a 55+ community builds equity and keeps property tax relief in play. Renting keeps money liquid and makes a later move easier. The right answer depends on your parent's health, savings and how long they expect to stay.

Buying usually means selling the family home first. Our downsizing guide covers the senior break on the realty transfer fee and how a move affects property tax relief. A senior move manager can handle the sorting and the move itself. Owners who pay property taxes on a condo or a home in a 55+ community count as homeowners for state relief programs. New Jersey Treasury treats someone who rents a condo or co-op unit as a renter. See our guide to ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ.

Renting fits a parent who wants services bundled in, or who may need more care within a few years. Get the full price list in writing: base rent, the monthly service fee, and charges for a second person, meals beyond the plan, parking, transportation and pets. Ask how much fees rose in each of the last three years. New Jersey landlords must give tenants the state's Truth in Renting guide, which explains tenant rights.

If your parent's income is limited, subsidized senior buildings are a different path with income limits and waiting lists. Our guide to affordable senior apartments explains how to apply.

What happens when your mom or dad needs more help?

In independent living, extra help is added from outside, or your parent moves. Neither a 55+ community nor a rental senior building is required to provide personal care.

Many families start by bringing in a home care agency. In New Jersey, agencies that place aides in the home are called health care service firms and are regulated by the Division of Consumer Affairs. Certified homemaker-home health aides are regulated by the New Jersey Board of Nursing. Our guide to choosing a home care agency walks through the checks. Simple home changes help too; see aging in place in New Jersey.

Ask every rental community what it does when a resident's needs change. Some ask residents to move once they need regular hands-on help. Get that policy in writing before move-in, along with the notice period. Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care in any setting. If money for care runs short later, New Jersey's Medicaid program for long-term care may help through its Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) program.

If your parent wants a promise of future care on the same campus, a continuing care retirement community is built for that, at a much higher upfront price.

What should we check before signing?

Visit more than once, read every document, and have someone you trust review the contract or purchase papers.

  1. Confirm the age rules. Ask for the written age policy and how the community verifies ages. Ask whether a younger spouse or caregiver can live there.
  2. Get every fee in writing. Monthly fee, what it covers, increases over the last three to five years, and any special assessments planned.
  3. Read the governing documents. For a purchase, read the master deed or declaration, bylaws, rules, budget and reserve study. Ask for recent board minutes.
  4. Ask what is not included. Meals, transportation, housekeeping, emergency call systems and who responds to them at night.
  5. Ask about changing needs. When would a renter be asked to leave? Can outside aides work in the building, and are there rules for them?
  6. Visit at different times. Go to a meal and an activity. Talk to residents without staff around.
  7. Get advice on the paperwork. A real estate attorney or an elder law attorney can review a purchase or a long lease. This guide is general information, not legal advice.

If your parent is in a rental building that is being converted to condominiums or a cooperative, the DCA Bureau of Homeowner Protection gives senior and disabled tenants information on applying for protected tenancy. Call 609-984-7905 to ask whether your parent may qualify.

faq.q: Can someone under 55 live in a 55+ community in New Jersey?
faq.a: Sometimes. Federal rules require only that at least 80 percent of occupied units have at least one resident 55 or older. Each community sets its own rule for the rest, so read its written age policy before buying.

faq.q: How do I find out if a 55+ community is legally age-restricted for my mom?
faq.a: Ask for its published age policy and how it verifies ages. Federal rules require age checks and an occupancy survey update at least once every two years, and a summary of those surveys must be available on reasonable request.

faq.q: Does independent living include help with bathing or medications?
faq.a: No. Independent living is housing with services like meals or activities. Personal care comes from an outside home care agency or a move to assisted living or a continuing care retirement community.

faq.q: Who do I call about a problem with a 55+ homeowners association in NJ?
faq.a: The DCA Bureau of Homeowner Protection at 609-984-7905. It can act on open meetings, access to financial records and dispute resolution procedures. It does not oversee fee increases, elections or management companies.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for independent living?
faq.a: No. Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care or housing. Your parent pays rent, fees or association dues from their own funds.

faq.q: How do I help my dad decide between renting and buying in a 55+ community?
faq.a: Compare how long he expects to stay, his health, and whether he wants services bundled in. Buying keeps homeowner property tax relief in play. Renting keeps savings liquid and makes a later move simpler.

title: Continuing care retirement communities (CCRCs) in New Jersey
dek: How New Jersey regulates CCRCs, what the disclosure statement and contract must say, refund and cancellation rights, and how to judge a community's finances.
keyFacts: NJ DCA certifies CCRCs under N.J.S.A. 52:27D-330 and following. Call 609-984-7905.
Residents can cancel within 30 days of signing for a full refund, minus the application fee.
After move-in, either side can end the contract with 60 days' notice; the CCRC needs just cause.
Providers must keep liquid reserves of at least 15% of yearly operating costs or 12 months of debt payments.
Fee increases need 30 days' written notice.
body:
A continuing care retirement community (CCRC) is a campus where your mom or dad moves into an apartment or cottage while still independent, under a contract that promises access to assisted living and nursing care later. Many now call themselves "life plan communities." In New Jersey, CCRCs that charge an entrance fee of at least 12 times the monthly fee are regulated by the Department of Community Affairs (DCA) under the Continuing Care Retirement Community Regulation and Financial Disclosure Act, N.J.S.A. 52:27D-330 and following.

That law gives families real protections. Your parent must get a disclosure statement before signing or paying. They have 30 days after signing to cancel for a full refund, minus the application fee. They can end the contract later with 60 days' notice. This guide explains each protection, the contract types and refund options, and how to judge a community's finances. It is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Who regulates CCRCs in New Jersey?

The DCA's Bureau of Homeowner Protection runs the state's CCRC Program. A community must register with DCA and hold a certificate of authority before it can sign continuing care contracts.

The DCA's consumer guidebook says certification means the state found that the provider can meet its contract obligations, its disclosure statement is complete, and its principals have no disqualifying criminal convictions or orders. DCA stresses that a certificate is not an endorsement.

The assisted living and nursing units on a CCRC campus are separately licensed by the New Jersey Department of Health. You can look them up, with inspection results, in the Department of Health facility search. Our guide to nursing home ratings explains how to read them.

The guidebook also points out a key line. The CCRC Act applies to communities whose entrance fee is at least 12 times the monthly service fee. A rental community with a small or no entrance fee may look similar but is not covered by the Act, so ask which state agency oversees it.

Check a CCRC's certificate

Call the DCA CCRC Program at 609-984-7905 to confirm a community holds a current certificate of authority. DCA's CCRC consumer guidebook (last revised in 2018) includes checklists and a county-by-county list, so confirm a community's current status by phone.

What is in a CCRC disclosure statement?

It is the community's full financial and legal picture, and your parent must receive it before signing a contract or handing over any money, whichever comes first. The standard contract is attached to it.

Under N.J.S.A. 52:27D-336, the disclosure statement must include:

  • Who owns and runs the community, their experience, and any business deals between insiders and the facility worth $500 or more a year.
  • Any affiliation with a religious or nonprofit group, and whether that group is responsible for the community's debts.
  • Every fee, how monthly fees can be raised, and a table of fee increases for up to the last five years.
  • Reserve funds, escrow accounts and who makes investment decisions.
  • Certified financial statements for the two most recent fiscal years.
  • For a community not yet built, construction costs, financing and projected occupancy.

The provider must file an updated statement with DCA every year, within six months after its fiscal year ends, and give the most current one to prospective residents. By law, the cover must carry a bold notice recommending that you consult an attorney and financial adviser before committing. A separate law gives your parent up to 30 days to review the disclosure statement and a plain-language explanation of resident rights before signing.

Ask for the disclosure statement on the first visit. A community that hesitates is telling you something.

What are the types of CCRC contracts?

DCA groups CCRC contracts into three basic plans: all-inclusive, modified and fee-for-service. Industry materials often call these Type A, Type B and Type C.

PlanFuture care
All-inclusive (A)Long-term nursing care as needed at no extra cost beyond inflation adjustments
Modified (B)Some care for a set time, then extra charges or a resident discount
Fee-for-service (C)Access guaranteed, paid at the going rate

All-inclusive plans usually carry the highest fees because residents pool the cost of future care. Fee-for-service plans cost less upfront, but a long nursing home stay could be paid out of pocket. Many communities offer more than one plan, with different entrance and monthly fees. Rental arrangements with no large entrance fee also exist, but as noted above they fall outside the CCRC Act.

If your parent has a long-term care insurance policy, ask how the community coordinates benefits with each plan.

How do entrance fees and refunds work?

There are three charges: an application fee, a one-time entrance fee and a monthly service fee. Refund terms depend on the contract your parent picks.

  • Application fee. DCA rules cap it at $500 unless the provider shows its actual processing cost is higher. It may not be refundable, so ask first.
  • Entrance fee. DCA notes that plans with a permanent refund usually cost more upfront than plans whose refund declines over time. The contract must state the refund terms in type no smaller than the largest type in the body of the agreement.
  • Monthly fee. Expect it to rise over time. The community must give 30 days' written notice before any increase.
  • Deposits on new buildings. On a project still being developed, a non-binding reservation deposit cannot exceed 10 percent of the entrance fee, is held in trust, and must be refunded if your parent cancels. State law requires entrance fees paid before move-in, above 5 percent, to be held in escrow under set rules.

Two money questions catch families off guard. First, Medicaid. Federal law (42 U.S.C. 1396p(g)) can count a refundable entrance fee as a resource when deciding Medicaid eligibility, if it can be used to pay for care and does not give an ownership interest. Second, taxes. IRS Publication 502 says part of a life-care or "founder's" fee that is properly allocated to medical care can count as a medical expense, using a statement from the community. Talk with a tax preparer, and see our guide to New Jersey retirement income tax.

A CCRC contract can also affect property tax relief. NJ Treasury treats a CCRC resident as a homeowner for its relief programs if the contract requires them to pay their share of the unit's property taxes.

Can your parent back out of a CCRC contract?

Yes. New Jersey law gives a 30-day window to cancel for a full refund, and a right to leave later with 60 days' notice.

  1. Within 30 days of signing. Your parent can cancel and get a full refund, except the application fee and any costs they asked for in a signed addendum. They do not have to move in before the 30 days are up.
  2. If they die or become unable to move in. If death, illness, injury or incapacity keeps them from moving in, the contract is automatically cancelled and all money is refunded, minus those same documented costs.
  3. After moving in. Either side can cancel with at least 60 days' notice. Any refund follows the contract's refund terms.
  4. If the community wants them out. It needs "just cause," such as a written good faith finding by the medical director and administrator that the resident is a danger to themselves or others. The resident can request a hearing.

Running short of money is not just cause until the unearned part of the entrance fee has been used up, under a formula in N.J.S.A. 52:27D-344. Even then, the community cannot require a resident to leave sooner than 90 days after the missed payment.

What rights do CCRC residents have in New Jersey?

New Jersey's Bill of Rights for Continuing Care Retirement Community Residents in Independent Living lists more than two dozen rights. Among them:

  • To stay in their chosen unit as long as they can live independently, with or without an aide.
  • To be told in writing of any right to appeal a finding that they can no longer live independently.
  • To choose their own doctor and to hire a private caregiver or companion at their own expense.
  • To get 30 days' notice before fee increases or cuts in services.
  • To organize and join a residents' association without reprisal.

The CCRC Act also requires the board or a designated representative to hold quarterly meetings with residents on finances and policy, with seven days' notice. The board must include at least one resident as a full voting member. If you have concerns about a resident's treatment, call the New Jersey Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995.

How do I check a CCRC's financial health?

Read the certified financial statements in the disclosure statement, and ask the community to walk you through them. State law sets a floor, and your job is to see how far above it the community sits.

Under N.J.S.A. 52:27D-339, each provider must keep liquid reserves at least equal to the greater of the next 12 months of mortgage principal and interest, or 15 percent of yearly operating expenses, not counting depreciation. Ask how much the community holds above that. Then ask:

  • What is occupancy in independent living, assisted living and nursing?
  • How have monthly fees risen over the last five years?
  • Is any debt being refinanced, or is new construction planned?
  • What happened when the provider's other communities, if any, had trouble?
  • Does the community carry a credit rating on its bonds?

Have an elder law attorney and a fee-only financial adviser review the disclosure statement and contract together. If your parent's needs are already beyond independent living, compare a CCRC with assisted living, or with staying in a smaller home. Our guide to independent living and 55+ communities covers the options without a care promise.

faq.q: How long does my mom have to cancel a CCRC contract in New Jersey?
faq.a: Thirty days after signing. She gets a full refund except the application fee and any costs she requested in a signed addendum, and she does not have to move in before the 30 days end.

faq.q: Who regulates continuing care retirement communities in NJ?
faq.a: The Department of Community Affairs CCRC Program, in the Bureau of Homeowner Protection, at 609-984-7905. The assisted living and nursing units on campus are also licensed by the Department of Health.

faq.q: What is a CCRC disclosure statement?
faq.a: A document the community must give before any contract is signed or money is paid. It covers ownership, all fees and past increases, reserves, and two years of certified financial statements, with the standard contract attached.

faq.q: Can a CCRC make my dad leave if he runs out of money?
faq.a: Not right away. New Jersey law says inability to pay monthly fees is not just cause until the unearned part of his entrance fee is used up, and he cannot be required to leave sooner than 90 days after the missed payment.

faq.q: Is a CCRC entrance fee refundable?
faq.a: It depends on the contract. Some plans refund a fixed share, some refund on a declining scale, and some refund little or nothing after a period. The contract must state the refund terms in large, clear print.

faq.q: Does Medicaid count a CCRC entrance fee as an asset?
faq.a: It can. Federal law treats a refundable entrance fee as a resource if it can be used to pay for care and does not give an ownership interest. Ask an elder law attorney before signing.

title: Senior living options in NJ: a plain guide to every choice
dek: From help at home to nursing homes, how each senior living option in New Jersey compares on care, cost, oversight and how families pay.
keyFacts: NJ medians (CareScout 2025): home care $38 an hour, assisted living $8,710 a month, semi-private nursing home $12,775 a month.
The NJ Department of Health licenses assisted living and nursing homes; the Department of Community Affairs registers CCRCs.
A 55+ community must have at least 80 percent of occupied units with a resident 55 or older.
Medicare does not pay for long-term care; NJ FamilyCare MLTSS can, for people who qualify.
Long-Term Care Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995.
body:
Older adults in New Jersey have eight main choices: staying home with paid help, adult day programs, independent living or a 55+ community, a continuing care retirement community (CCRC), assisted living, memory care, a nursing home, and affordable senior apartments. The right one depends on three things. How much help your mom or dad needs each day, whether they are safe alone at night, and what the family can afford over several years.

Costs run from a few hundred dollars a month for some help at home to more than $14,000 a month for a private nursing home room. This page compares every option side by side and links to a detailed guide for each one, so you can narrow the list before you tour anything.

How do the options compare?

Start with the level of care. Then check cost and who oversees the setting.

OptionFits someone who
Home with helpWants to stay put, needs some hours of help
Adult dayLives at home, should not be alone all day
Independent living or 55+Needs no daily care, wants less upkeep
CCRCIs independent now, wants care on site later
Assisted livingNeeds help with bathing, dressing or pills
Memory careHas dementia and needs a secure setting
Nursing homeNeeds 24-hour nursing care
Senior apartmentsLives independently on a limited income
OptionNJ median cost
Home care$38 an hour
Adult day health$100 a day
Assisted living$8,710 a month
Nursing home, shared$12,775 a month
Nursing home, private$14,448 a month

Costs are New Jersey medians from the CareScout Cost of Care Survey 2025, collected July through November 2025. CareScout does not report independent living, CCRC or memory care costs. Those vary widely by community, so get each price in writing. For more detail, see what senior care costs in New Jersey.

Which option fits my parent right now?

Match the setting to the need you see today, and keep the next likely step in mind. These questions sort most families quickly.

  • Is your parent safe alone overnight? If yes, home with help, adult day or independent living may work. If not, you are looking at round-the-clock help at home, assisted living, memory care or a nursing home.
  • Does your parent need hands-on help with bathing, dressing or the toilet? Independent living and 55+ communities do not provide that. Assisted living does.
  • Is there wandering, getting lost or unsafe behavior from dementia? Ask about secured memory care. Our memory care guide covers what to look for.
  • Are there heavy medical needs, like lifting help, wounds or complex medications? A nursing home may be the safer fit.
  • Is the main problem loneliness or upkeep? A move to a 55+ community, a senior apartment or adding adult day can solve that without care services.
Choose for the need you see today, then ask each place what happens when that need grows.

Can my parent stay home with help?

Often, yes. Home care is the cheapest option when the need is a few hours a day. It gets expensive as hours climb. At the median $38 an hour, 44 hours a week is $7,245 a month, before the cost of running the house.

Help with the bill can come from several places. NJ FamilyCare's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) program pays for care at home for people who need a nursing home level of care and meet the financial rules. The state-funded JACC program serves people 60 and older at home who need a nursing home level of care and are not on Medicaid. Our guides to aging in place, choosing a home care agency and JACC explain each one.

What does adult day add?

Adult day gives your parent a safe, social place during the day and gives a working caregiver coverage. It is often the step that keeps someone home longer.

New Jersey has two kinds. Adult day health services, also called medical day care, are licensed by the NJ Department of Health and have nursing on site. Social adult day programs offer supervision and activities without medical care. The New Jersey median for adult day health care is $100 a day, or about $2,167 a month at five days a week. MLTSS can cover adult day health for members. Our adult day care guide covers both types and other ways to pay.

What is the difference between independent living, 55+ communities and a CCRC?

None of the three provides daily hands-on care as part of the basic arrangement, except that a CCRC adds care levels on the same campus for later.

  • 55+ communities are homes or condos, usually bought. Under the federal Housing for Older Persons Act, one requirement for a 55+ community is that at least 80 percent of occupied units have at least one resident 55 or older. An association runs shared spaces and charges fees.
  • Independent living is usually a rental apartment building for older adults, with meals, activities and housekeeping often included in the monthly rent. Care is added separately, often through a home care agency.
  • A CCRC offers independent living, assisted living and nursing care on one campus, usually for an entrance fee plus a monthly fee. New Jersey's Department of Community Affairs registers CCRCs under the Continuing Care Retirement Community Regulation and Financial Disclosure Act, and each must prepare a Disclosure Statement on its services, fees, finances and contract terms.

Read our guides to independent living and 55+ communities and CCRCs in New Jersey for contract types, fees and questions to ask.

When is assisted living, memory care or a nursing home the right step?

When help is needed through the day and night. Assisted living suits someone who needs daily help but not round-the-clock nursing. Memory care suits someone with dementia who needs a secure setting. A nursing home suits someone with heavy medical or physical needs.

The NJ Department of Health licenses assisted living residences, comprehensive personal care homes and assisted living programs under N.J.A.C. 8:36, and it licenses nursing homes too. Memory care is often a secured unit inside an assisted living residence or nursing home. The 2025 New Jersey medians are $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom in assisted living and $12,775 a month for a semi-private nursing home room.

Medicare does not pay for long-term care in any of these settings. It covers up to 100 days in a skilled nursing facility per benefit period after a qualifying hospital stay, and in 2026 days 21 to 100 cost $217 a day. MLTSS can pay for long-term nursing home care and for care in assisted living residences that accept Medicaid. Not all of them do, so ask before your parent moves in.

Our detailed guides: assisted living in New Jersey and nursing home vs. memory care, which also covers how to check a nursing home.

What if money is tight?

Two paths help most. Subsidized senior apartments lower housing costs for people who can live on their own. Medicaid's MLTSS pays for care once savings are low.

HUD's Section 202 program funds apartment buildings for very low income households with someone 62 or older, generally under 50 percent of the area median income. Public housing and Housing Choice Vouchers can also help. Waiting lists are long, so apply to several at once. Our affordable senior apartments guide walks through each one.

For care costs, the 2026 MLTSS income limit is $2,982 a month and a single person can keep $2,000 in countable resources, with the home and the car used not counted. Medicaid reviews five years of finances. Read paying for long-term care in New Jersey before your parent spends down or gives anything away. This is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Who can help us decide?

You do not have to sort this out alone. Free public help is available in every county.

  1. Call your county's Area Agency on Aging. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection connects you at 1-877-222-3737. Staff can explain local options and schedule a Medicaid screening.
  2. Get a clear picture of needs. Ask your parent's doctor what level of care they think is safe. A geriatric care manager can do a fuller assessment for a fee.
  3. List two or three options that fit, using the tables above, and get written prices from each place.
  4. Check licenses and records. Use the NJ Department of Health's facility search for licensed settings, and ask each place about recent inspections.
  5. Decide how you will search. Some families use a placement service. Read our guide to senior living placement services first so you know how they are paid.
  6. Plan the move. Our housing choices guide has a touring checklist. A senior move manager can help with packing and downsizing.
If something goes wrong after the move

The New Jersey Long-Term Care Ombudsman advocates for residents of nursing homes, assisted living, adult day centers and the independent living section of CCRCs. Call 1-877-582-6995. Complaints about care in a facility licensed by the Department of Health can also go to 1-800-792-9770. In an emergency, call 911.

faq.q: How do I know which kind of senior living my mom needs?
faq.a: Start with two questions. Is she safe alone overnight, and does she need hands-on help with bathing, dressing or the toilet? If she is safe and independent, help at home, adult day or independent living may be enough. If not, look at assisted living, memory care or a nursing home. Her doctor or your county Area Agency on Aging (1-877-222-3737) can help you judge.

faq.q: What is the difference between independent living and assisted living?
faq.a: Independent living is housing with services like meals and activities but no daily hands-on care. Assisted living is licensed by the NJ Department of Health and provides help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing and medications, with staff on site around the clock.

faq.q: What is the cheapest senior living option in New Jersey?
faq.a: For someone who can live on their own with a limited income, subsidized senior apartments usually cost the least, since rent is typically based on income. For someone who needs care, a few hours of home care or adult day is cheaper than a facility. Full-time care at home can cost as much as assisted living.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for assisted living or a nursing home?
faq.a: Medicare does not pay for long-term care. It covers up to 100 days of skilled nursing facility care per benefit period after a qualifying hospital stay, with a $217 daily coinsurance for days 21 to 100 in 2026. NJ FamilyCare MLTSS can pay for long-term care for people who meet its medical and financial rules.

faq.q: How can I find out if a facility near my dad has had problems?
faq.a: Use the NJ Department of Health's facility search to confirm the license, ask the facility about recent inspections, and read our nursing home ratings guide. To raise a concern about a resident's care, call the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995 or the Department of Health complaint line at 1-800-792-9770.
